duration: Extended to a one-year moratorium on 2026-07-14; reported to run into June 2027 while the County's advisory committee develops recommendations.

current_status: Rescinded by court order as of 2026-09-23. Imperial County Superior Court Judge Jeffrey B. Jones entered judgment 2026-09-04 in favor of developer Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC, finding neither Ordinance 1616 (the original moratorium) nor Ordinance 1618 (its ~10-month-15-day extension) made the causal finding of a 'current and immediate threat to public health, safety, or welfare' required by Gov. Code section 65858. A peremptory writ of mandate issued 2026-09-11 directs the County and Board of Supervisors to set aside both ordinances and stop using them to withhold, suspend, or refuse data-center permits. The County has said (per KYMA, 2026-09-22) it is working on a new moratorium addressing the court's concerns; no replacement had been adopted as of 2026-09-23. The Data Center Advisory Committee, created alongside the moratorium, continues to meet (inaugural meeting 2026-09-17) and is unaffected by the ruling. Separately, a different judge (L. Brooks Anderholt) has ordered a full CEQA environmental review of the underlying data center project in a related case, so the project itself remains stalled notwithstanding the moratorium's invalidation.
affected_projects: A proposed large-scale data center complex; the developer (reported as Sebastian Rucci) indicated plans to challenge the decision in court.
outcome: Moratorium (Ordinances 1616 and 1618) adopted and extended to run through mid-2027, then invalidated by the Imperial County Superior Court (Judge Jeffrey B. Jones) in Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC v. County of Imperial: judgment entered 2026-09-04, peremptory writ of mandate issued 2026-09-11 ordering the County to set aside and cease enforcing both ordinances because their findings did not satisfy Gov. Code section 65858's 'current and immediate threat' standard. The County has 30 days after service of the writ to file a return; county officials say they are preparing a new moratorium that addresses the court's findings. The Data Center Advisory Committee process continues separately.

legal_basis: Town of Cedaredge Ordinance No. 2026-07 (renumbered from the originally recorded 2026-06 per the Board's 09/17/2026-amended Record of Proceedings)
trigger: Board referral by Trustee Hoffbauer under Trustee Comments on 8/6/2026, citing lack of adequate local standards for data center facilities; expedited as an emergency ordinance given potential impacts on Town water supply and availability.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Emergency moratorium adopted 6-1 on August 20, 2026 (Ordinance No. 2026-07), running through the earlier of February 20, 2027 or adoption of permanent data-center standards.
affected_projects: None; the ordinance recites that 'there are no pending applications for a data center facility to be developed within the Town.'
outcome: Board of Trustees adopted an emergency six-month moratorium on data center applications in all zoning districts, following the path of Delta County and the Town of Paonia.

legal_basis: Draft Commerce City ordinance considered at a regularly scheduled City Council meeting (specific date and ordinance number not confirmed in this pass; reported as a 'Monday night' vote in coverage published September 22, 2026)
trigger: City staff cited significant potential impacts of data centers on city infrastructure (power and water supply), neighborhood character, and surrounding land use, given the land development code's silence on data-center-specific standards.
current_status: Pending as of 2026-09-23. City Council was considering (per news coverage published September 22, 2026, referring to a 'Monday night' vote) a six-month moratorium on data center development plan and zoning applications; the outcome of that vote was not confirmed in sources available as of the research date. affected_projects: None named.
outcome: City Council considered a staff-recommended six-month moratorium on data center development applications; adoption status as of 2026-09-23 was not confirmed.

date_enacted: Board of County Commissioners adopted Resolution R-18 on 2026-07-07.
duration: Temporary moratorium on data center facility applications in unincorporated Delta County, covering pre-submittal activity and planning, building, engineering, and other development applications. Scheduled to expire January 7, 2027, or when the county adopts permanent regulations, whichever occurs first.
legal_basis: Delta County Resolution R-18
trigger: County review will consider land-use compatibility, water and energy demand, infrastructure, noise, environmental effects, emergency response, and economic development.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Confirmed via Delta County's own official website: Resolution R-18 'is scheduled to remain in effect until January 7, 2027, or until the County completes and adopts appropriate regulations, whichever occurs first.' County Commissioners' regular meetings through at least September 1, 2026 (reported September 7, 2026) show the related Land Use Code review (covering natural medicine and battery-storage standards, not data centers) still under way with no final action, and no repeal or early replacement of the data-center moratorium.

date_enacted: 2026-05-18 (City Council final passage of Council Bill 26-0431 at second reading/public hearing, unanimous); signed by the Mayor 2026-05-20; effective 2026-05-21
duration: One year from the effective date (2026-05-21, i.e. nominally through 2027-05-21), or upon adoption of amendments to the Denver Revised Municipal Code and a text amendment to the Denver Zoning Code addressing data centers, per Section 5 of the ordinance as filed and passed without amendment to that section: 'This moratorium shall expire the earlier of: (a) One year from the effective date of this ordinance; or (b) The effective date of any amendments to the Denver Revised Municipal Code regarding data centers and any text amendment to the Denver Zoning Code regarding data centers, whichever occurs later.' (The 'earlier of ... whichever occurs later' phrasing is the ordinance's own internal drafting inconsistency, quoted verbatim.)
legal_basis: Council Bill 26-0431 (Series of 2026), passed by City Council on final consideration 2026-05-18 and signed by the Mayor 2026-05-20; effective 2026-05-21. Denver's own official city government page ('Data Centers in Denver,' denvergov.org) and its Legistar record both cite 'CB 26-0431' / 'Ordinance 26-0431' as the enactment's operative citation; no separate sequential codified ordinance number distinct from the council bill number was found, and the city's own public FAQ page uses '26-0431' as the identifier when explaining the moratorium to residents.
trigger: No data-center-specific zoning regulations; concerns about water, energy, ratepayer cost shifting, noise, air quality, siting, and impacts on vulnerable communities.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Denver's own official city page confirms the moratorium runs 'from May 21, 2026 to May 21, 2027.' The city has begun forming a 20+ member community Working Group (facilitated by Group14 Engineering and the Civic Consulting Collaborative) to recommend post-moratorium zoning, building, and energy code changes; applications were open August 21-September 4, 2026, and the Working Group's first meeting is scheduled for October 9, 2026. Denver's own page states the moratorium 'will be extended' if the Working Group needs more time. No repeal, early amendment, or Denver Zoning Code/Municipal Code data-center text amendment that would end the moratorium early was found as of 2026-09-23.
affected_projects: Existing and already permitted projects would not be stopped. CoreSite DE3 phase one at 4900 Race Street is under construction; future phases had not been permitted as of captured reporting.
outcome: If enacted, Denver would use the pause for a working group and possible amendments to zoning, building, energy, green/climate, and municipal code provisions.

date_enacted: Board of County Commissioners approved at its June 9, 2026 meeting in Hot Sulphur Springs.
duration: Moratorium on construction of data centers under the county's state-delegated 1041 authority, deliberately aligned to expire on the same date as the county's existing two-year moratorium on commercial/utility-scale solar and wind facilities over 25 kW (adopted June 24, 2025).
legal_basis: Grand County Board of County Commissioners resolution under its state-delegated 1041 regulatory authority (specific resolution number not located in this pass)
trigger: Commissioners determined data centers fall under the same 1041 category as solar/wind facilities and should be reviewed together; no existing data center regulations in the county.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Moratorium on data center construction adopted June 9, 2026, aligned to expire June 24, 2027 alongside the county's existing solar/wind moratorium. affected_projects: None named.
outcome: Board of County Commissioners adopted a moratorium on data center construction under its 1041 powers, to run concurrently with the county's existing solar/wind facility moratorium.

duration: Ten-month moratorium adopted at a May 19, 2026 public hearing on new applications for development of, or rezoning to allow, data centers in unincorporated Jefferson County; excludes land already zoned for data centers via a Planned Development at least 1,500 feet from any dwelling. Runs through approximately March 19, 2027.
legal_basis: Jefferson County Board of County Commissioners action taken at a public hearing on May 19, 2026, per the County's own official jeffco.us news release; a numbered resolution/ordinance citation was not published in that release or located elsewhere in this pass.
trigger: Commissioners cited the need to evaluate how data centers interact with the Wildland Urban Interface (WUI), the county's water supply, environment, and community health, while weighing potential job growth against community impact (per the county's official news release).
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Ten-month moratorium on new data center development and rezoning applications in unincorporated Jefferson County, adopted at a May 19, 2026 public hearing (confirmed via the County's own official news release), running through approximately March 19, 2027 unless ended sooner. No repeal or extension found.
affected_projects: Not specified in the source reviewed.
outcome: County weighing environmental impacts against economic benefits before allowing new data center applications.

date_enacted: Town Council passed Ordinance 2026-295 on a 5-1 vote at its Monday, July 20, 2026 meeting (Mayor Duncan, Mayor Pro Tem Young, and Councilmembers Berg, Morris, and Menzies voting aye; Councilmember Bashford opposed; Councilmember Molinar absent).
duration: 12-month moratorium (or until Johnstown adopts data-center definitions, standards, regulations, and conditions into its Land Use Development Code, whichever is first) on accepting applications or engaging in pre-submittal activities for data-center facilities, including planning applications, building permits, and engineering permits.
legal_basis: Town of Johnstown Ordinance 2026-295
trigger: Town officials cited the lack of comprehensive zoning, land-use, or water-management regulations addressing data centers' potential burden on the town's long-term energy, water, and fiber resources; no data center project has been proposed in Johnstown.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. 12-month moratorium on data center facility applications, adopted 5-1 on July 20, 2026 via Ordinance 2026-295.
affected_projects: None; no data center project has been approved or proposed in Johnstown.
outcome: Town Council adopted a 12-month moratorium on data-center facility applications, with Councilmember Bashford dissenting on grounds it represented government overreach.

duration: Initial 30 days from 2026-01-27 (Resolution, Reception No. 20260005307); extended six months to 2026-08-25 by a resolution signed 2026-04-07 (Reception No. 20260016505), following a 2026-02-09 public hearing; extended a second time, six more months, to 2026-02-25 (2027), by a resolution signed 2026-07-13 (Reception No. 20260034886), following a 2026-07-13 public hearing.
legal_basis: Resolution to Establish a Temporary Moratorium on Data Center Facilities in Larimer County, Colorado, signed 2026-01-27, Larimer County Clerk & Recorder Reception No. 20260005307 (initial 30 days); Resolution to Establish a Temporary Moratorium on Data Center Facilities in Larimer County, Colorado (extension), signed 2026-04-07, Reception No. 20260016505 (extends through 2026-08-25, following the 2026-02-09 hearing); Resolution to Extend the Temporary Moratorium on Data Center Facilities in Larimer County, Colorado, signed 2026-07-13, Reception No. 20260034886 (extends through 2026-02-25, 2027, following the 2026-07-13 hearing). Authority cited: C.R.S. section 30-28-121 (temporary regulations, not to exceed six months).
trigger: Larimer County Land Use Code had no definitions or regulations for data center uses; county cited water consumption, power usage, noise, aesthetics, heat effects, and suitable zoning.
current_status: Active through 2026-02-25, 2027, per a second extension resolution signed 2026-07-13 (recorded 2026-07-14, Clerk & Recorder Reception No. 20260034886), following a 2026-07-13 public hearing. No Land Use Code amendments addressing data centers had been adopted as of that extension; a public survey that closed 2026-06-12 reportedly found 94% of respondents opposed to data center construction.
affected_projects: No site-specific data center applications had been submitted as of the county's 2026-04-23 update.
outcome: County is drafting Land Use Code definitions and standards and opened a public survey through 2026-06-12.

date_enacted: Town Board voted 6-1 on July 21, 2026 to approve an ordinance introduced by Mayor Jamie Jeffery.
duration: Five-year pause on the Town's acceptance and review of applications for new or expanded data center facilities -- reported as the longest active data-center moratorium in Colorado.
legal_basis: Town of Lochbuie ordinance (specific ordinance number not located in this pass), adopted July 21, 2026
trigger: Preemptive action; no data center has been proposed in Lochbuie, but a large data center (Cielo Hudson Data Center, ~500 acres/750 MW) is planned in neighboring Hudson. Over 400 residents petitioned via an Action Network campaign organized by the nonprofit 'With Many Hands,' citing water and electricity concerns amid statewide drought.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Five-year moratorium on new/expanded data center facility applications, adopted 6-1 on July 21, 2026.
affected_projects: None proposed within Lochbuie; cited concern is the neighboring Cielo Hudson Data Center project in the Town of Hudson.
outcome: Town Board passed a five-year moratorium on data center applications, the longest such pause reported in Colorado.

duration: 180 days as adopted; replaced by Resolution 2026-5 (effective 2026-02-17) before the full term elapsed
legal_basis: Resolution 2025-25
trigger: County needed time to draft regulations before accepting or processing applications for data center, battery, solar, and wind facilities; meeting records cited grid, infrastructure, agricultural land, and land use compatibility concerns.
current_status: Replaced. All four facility types covered by Resolution 2025-25 were superseded by their own permanent regulation resolutions, each with an explicit rescission clause tied back to Resolution 2025-25: Resolution 2026-4 (Battery Energy Storage Systems, effective 2026-02-17), Resolution 2026-5 (Data Center Facilities, effective 2026-02-17), Resolution 2026-6 (Solar Energy / Community Solar Garden, effective 2026-02-17), and Resolution 2026-11 (Wind Energy Facilities, adopted 2026-04-07, shortly before the moratorium's own ~2026-04-19 lapse date). None of the four components lapsed unaddressed.
affected_projects: County Commissioners' October 14, 2025 work-session minutes record a briefing by developer Blake Marcus (Granite Renewables) and consultant Ben Gager (SWCA Environmental Consultants) describing a proposed project east and west of County Road 9 (approximately 21 miles northwest of Sterling) at close to 2 GW nameplate capacity, including 1 GW of on-site natural gas generation, 630 MW of solar as ancillary power, and 1,800 MWh of battery storage. Commissioner Yahn noted the moratorium had already been planned before this specific proposal surfaced. As of a January 2026 hearing, commissioners stated no formal permit application had yet been received.
outcome: Resolution 2026-5 adopted Data Center Facility regulations. The county planning page lists Resolution 2026-5 among amended regulations effective 2026-02-17 and 2026-04-07.

date_enacted: City Council voted 7-2 on September 15, 2026 to adopt the suspension, after amending the staff-proposed 9-month term to 12 months on a 5-4 vote (Councilor Laura Light-Kovacs' motion).
duration: 12-month suspension on the City's acceptance, processing, approval, permitting, rezoning, and site plan review of new land use applications for data centers with an electrical demand of 10 MW or more or that use industrial-scale cooling infrastructure; ends upon adoption of comprehensive Unified Development Code data-center regulations or 12 months from the effective date, whichever is first.
legal_basis: City of Loveland Resolution (number not assigned in the draft text reviewed; adopted September 15, 2026)
trigger: No pending applications, but staff and council cited the lack of statewide regulation after SB26-102 and HB26-1030 were both postponed indefinitely, and the need for the City to coordinate with the Platte River Power Authority on grid impacts and study water/cooling tradeoffs.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. 12-month suspension on large-scale data center land use applications, adopted 7-2 on September 15, 2026, effective immediately, running through approximately September 15, 2027 unless data-center regulations are adopted sooner.
affected_projects: None named; Loveland had not received a formal data center application as of adoption, though the city acknowledged informal developer interest.
outcome: City Council approved a 12-month suspension on large-scale data center development applications while staff develop permanent land use regulations.

date_enacted: Board of Trustees approved on a 4-2 vote (Trustees Hagan and Crane dissenting) at its August 31, 2026 meeting.
duration: 12-month moratorium preventing data centers from applying to develop in Mead; does not permanently prohibit data centers, and can end sooner than 12 months if staff has adequate information to develop regulations.
legal_basis: Town of Mead ordinance (specific ordinance number not located in this pass), adopted August 31, 2026
trigger: Town Attorney Marcus McAskin cited increasing interest in Front Range data center development (e.g., the proposed Global AI facility in Windsor) and substantial potential demands on electrical power, utility infrastructure, and water supply.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. 12-month moratorium on data center development applications, adopted 4-2 on August 31, 2026.
affected_projects: None in Mead; cited concern is the broader Front Range trend, including the proposed Global AI data center in nearby Windsor.
outcome: Board of Trustees approved a 12-month moratorium on data center applications to give staff time to study impacts and develop regulations.

date_enacted: Board of Trustees introduced/discussed at its May 27, 2026 regular meeting; the Town's own Municode ordinance index records final adoption as Ordinance No. 2026-839 on 7/30/2026.
duration: One-year moratorium on accepting/processing applications for data center uses, to give town staff time to research and develop land use regulations.
legal_basis: Town of Milliken Ordinance No. 2026-839, 'AN ORDINANCE OF THE TOWN OF MILLIKEN, COLORADO, APPROVING A MORATORIUM ON ACCEPTANCE AND PROCESSING OF APPLICATIONS FOR DATA CENTER USES,' per the Town's official Municode ordinance index
trigger: Not specified in the sources reviewed beyond the general statewide pattern of pausing applications pending land use regulation development.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. One-year moratorium on data center use applications, formally adopted July 30, 2026 as Ordinance No. 2026-839, following initial Board discussion/passage at the May 27, 2026 meeting.
affected_projects: None named.
outcome: Board of Trustees adopted a one-year moratorium on accepting and processing data center use applications while staff research land use regulations.

trigger: The county's Zoning Resolution does not currently contain specific regulations, standards, or definitions addressing data center facilities' impacts on electrical power, water supply, telecommunications, and transportation infrastructure.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Six-month moratorium under Resolution 23-2026, effective July 1, 2026, on data center facility applications in unincorporated Montrose County.
affected_projects: None named.

date_enacted: Town Council voted 6-0 to adopt Ordinance 18-2026 on 2026-07-20.
duration: Six-month moratorium on permit and land-development applications that include a data center as a principal or accessory use.
legal_basis: Town of Monument Ordinance 18-2026
trigger: No data center proposal was pending; staff planned to address data centers in a broader rewrite of the land-development code.
current_status: Active six-month moratorium.

duration: One-year moratorium tied to Resolution 15-26, refusing data center applications until August 11, 2027; also directs staff to draft a data-center-specific ordinance.
legal_basis: Town of Paonia Resolution 15-26

current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. One-year moratorium under Resolution 15-26, adopted August 11, 2026, refusing data center applications through August 11, 2027.
affected_projects: None named; adopted preemptively, citing Delta County's similar moratorium.

legal_basis: Saguache County Board of County Commissioners emergency resolution (specific resolution number not located in this pass), adopted May 5, 2026

date_enacted: The Town Board of the Town of South Fork introduced and passed Emergency Ordinance No. 2026-03 on June 18, 2026, per the archived legal notice published in the Valley Courier's July 1, 2026 edition. The notice's own adoption clause misstates the enacting body as 'Town of Center,' which is judged to be a drafting/scrivener error: every other part of the notice -- its heading ('TOWN OF SOUTH FORK'), all WHEREAS recitals, and the operative sections (which reference amending 'the South Fork Revised Municipal Code' and 'the South Fork Zoning Code') -- identifies the Town of South Fork, and the neighboring Town of Center's own published board-meeting calendar shows no meeting on June 18, 2026 at all.
duration: One-year pause on permit and site-development applications for new primary-use data centers while the town considers code amendments and community engagement.
legal_basis: Town of South Fork Emergency Ordinance No. 2026-03. The ordinance's own adoption clause names 'Town of Center' rather than South Fork, but this is judged a scrivener's error (see date_enacted): the heading, every recital, and every operative section name South Fork, and the Town of Center's own agenda calendar (via towncloud.io) shows no board meeting on June 18, 2026.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; jurisdiction confirmed as the Town of South Fork (see legal_basis). Per Section 4 of the ordinance, the one-year pause on data center site-development and permit applications expires the earlier of June 18, 2027, or the effective date of South Fork Revised Municipal Code/Zoning Code amendments addressing data centers, whichever occurs later (the ordinance's own internal 'earlier of ... whichever occurs later' drafting, quoted verbatim). No repeal or amendment found.

date_enacted: City Council adopted Ordinance 1525 on 2026-07-16, following a first reading on 2026-06-18.
duration: Pauses submission, acceptance, processing, review, hearings, approval, and siting of new or expanded data centers while the city develops definitions and land-use, water, and wastewater rules. City Council passed Ordinance No. 1525 (Series 2026) on second/final reading July 16, 2026 as an 18-month moratorium: The Gazette's July 17, 2026 report of that meeting states 'The 18-month moratorium halts data centers' and quotes Councilmember Seth Bryant explaining why council chose 18 rather than 12 months. The city's posted first-reading document (posted June 19, 2026, before the amendment) still shows the pre-amendment 12-month figure and blank termination-date placeholders; a signed second-reading ordinance with the filled-in date was not located, but the 18-month figure is independently corroborated by Colorado Newsline and the Denver Gazette.
legal_basis: City of Woodland Park Ordinance 1525 (Series 2026)
trigger: No data center proposal was pending at the time of adoption; described as a proactive measure.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Adopted 2026-07-16 as an 18-month moratorium (through approximately 2028-01-16), confirmed by The Gazette's July 17, 2026 report of the second-reading vote and corroborated by Colorado Newsline (August 10, 2026) and the Denver Gazette (September 12, 2026). No repeal or amendment found.

date_enacted: Not yet adopted as of 2026-09-23. Application #26-25 (a text amendment to Cromwell Zoning Regulations Section 4.2.E. to impose a 12-month moratorium on data centers) was introduced by Planning and Zoning Commission Chair Kelly; on 2026-08-18 the Commission voted 5-1 (Commissioner Michael Cannata dissenting) only to accept the application and schedule it for a public hearing at a Special Meeting on 2026-09-24 -- one day after this research date.
duration: Proposed 12 months
legal_basis: Proposed text amendment (Application #26-25) to Cromwell Zoning Regulations Section 4.2.E.; not yet adopted. Public hearing scheduled for a Special Meeting of the Planning and Zoning Commission on 2026-09-24.
trigger: regulatory_gap: the town's zoning regulations have no definition or standards for a data center use; the moratorium proposal was introduced to pause any data center application while regulations are developed alongside a broader, already-contracted zoning-regulations rewrite (consultant IMEG). Commissioner Cannata opposed the moratorium, citing an unnamed prospective applicant who has worked with the town for nine months and already secured a property option.
current_status: Pending as of 2026-09-23. At its August 18, 2026 regular meeting, the Cromwell Planning and Zoning Commission voted 5-1 to accept Application #26-25 (the proposed 12-month data center moratorium text amendment) and schedule it for a public hearing at a Special Meeting on September 24, 2026 -- the Commission did not adopt the moratorium at the August 18 meeting itself. Staff confirmed no data center application is currently pending, though one commissioner referenced an interested prospective applicant. A secondary aggregator (mytownview.com) inaccurately described this August 18 procedural vote as the Commission having 'approved' and 'passed' the moratorium itself; the official filed minutes make clear only the scheduling of a hearing was voted on.
affected_projects: An unnamed prospective data center applicant, described by Commissioner Cannata as having worked with the town for approximately nine months and secured an option on a property, was cited during discussion; no formal application has been filed.
outcome: Planning and Zoning Commission voted 5-1 to schedule a public hearing (Sept. 24, 2026) on a proposed 12-month data center moratorium text amendment; the moratorium itself has not been adopted as of this research date.

duration: One year

current_status: Replaced

duration: 12 months from effective date of adoption

The Commission's own document repository shows the moratorium text moved from a 'generals' (draft/agenda-attachment) filing on 2026-04-15 to a 'regulations' filing dated 2026-05-20, and secondary press reports the Commission approved the moratorium following a public hearing in mid-May 2026. The operative text (Section 6) fixes a 12-month term running from the effective date of adoption, notwithstanding press descriptions of it as a 'two-year moratorium' (which do not match the adopted text I read).

outcome: Pending; moratorium directs the commission to prepare zoning amendments as appropriate

date_enacted: Introduced 2026-07-06 as a communication by Board of Alders Majority Leader Richard Furlow (item LM-2026-0285). The item was on the full Board of Alders' agenda for its 2026-09-08 meeting (a Tuesday, since the Board's usual Monday date fell on Labor Day). Yale Daily News reported the Board voted unanimously that Tuesday to adopt the 12-month moratorium; this is treated as the adoption date, though it could not be independently corroborated with a second source (see notes on residual uncertainty).
duration: 12 months from adoption (ordinance text: 'A TEMPORARY TWELVE (12) MONTH MORATORIUM ON DATA CENTER DEVELOPMENT WITHIN THE CITY OF NEW HAVEN'), per the official ordinance language on file with the City/Town Clerk (Legistar file LM-2026-0285).
legal_basis: Ordinance Amendment of the New Haven Board of Alders establishing a temporary twelve (12) month moratorium on data center development within the City of New Haven (Legistar file LM-2026-0285), introduced 2026-07-06, Legislation Committee Favorable Report 2026-08-04, before the full Board of Alders 2026-09-08.
trigger: Proactive/regulatory-gap: the city has no zoning framework for data centers and wants to develop one before any project is proposed, drawing on approaches used by Groton, Morris, and West Haven, Connecticut.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23 (moderate confidence). The Legislation Committee gave a Favorable Report on 2026-08-04 and the item (LM-2026-0285) was on the full Board of Alders' September 8, 2026 agenda. Yale Daily News reported (headline and lede snippet) that the Board voted unanimously that Tuesday to adopt the 12-month data center moratorium. This could not be independently corroborated: the Yale Daily News article itself returned a bot-detection (Kasada) challenge on both a direct and a browser-mode fetch, so only the search-engine snippet could be read; New Haven Independent, which had covered every earlier stage of this item in detail, published no follow-up story on the Sept. 8 vote; and the official September 8, 2026 Board of Alders meeting agenda (fetched directly from newhaven-ct.legistar.com) groups LM-2026-0285 together with several unrelated items under a 'Legislation. Leave to withdraw' heading, which -- taken literally -- would mean the Legislation Committee's report on this batch recommended withdrawal rather than passage. This agenda-formatting ambiguity is inconsistent with the item's own recorded 8/4/2026 'Favorable Report' status and could reflect a template/carryover artifact in how the city's agenda software groups items, rather than an actual disposition of LM-2026-0285 specifically. Because no direct, unambiguous confirmation of the final vote result could be obtained, this decision is recorded with moderate rather than high confidence.
affected_projects: None. New Haven's Deputy Director of Zoning stated there are no current proposals or plans by any entity to build a data center in New Haven.
outcome: Proposed 12-month moratorium to allow the city's economic development department to convene a working group evaluating opportunities and impacts before any zoning framework is adopted.

date_enacted: 2026-09-09, Trumbull Town Council, unanimous voice vote at a public hearing/regular meeting
duration: 2 years, effective immediately upon adoption
legal_basis: Resolution TC31-65 (Trumbull Town Council), amending the Trumbull Municipal Code: 'The Town hereby adopts a two-year moratorium on the establishment and development of any new data centers within the Town of Trumbull.' Public hearing held at the same September 9, 2026 Town Council meeting.
trigger: specific_project concerns: 365 Data Centers (Norwalk) and Aphorio Carter (a data center division of private equity firm Carter Funds) announced in May 2026 plans for a 200 MW pipeline of AI-ready data centers, naming Trumbull's decades-old former Nasdaq data center at 80 Merritt Blvd. as a likely site for modernization into a 'high density, AI-ready' facility; a resident petition and advocacy group (Trumbull AI Data Center Watch) pushed for a moratorium and had sought (unsuccessfully) to have it cover the 80 Merritt Blvd. project itself.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. The Town Council unanimously adopted Resolution TC31-65 on 2026-09-09, imposing a 2-year moratorium (effective immediately) on the 'establishment and development' of any new data centers in Trumbull. The moratorium does NOT apply to the modernization/upgrade of the town's existing 80 Merritt Blvd. data center (a 15 MW facility in operation 50+ years, now being converted to AI-ready use by 365 Data Centers), which the town characterizes as a renovation rather than new construction; residents have petitioned unsuccessfully to have that project included and are considering a signature drive (requiring roughly 2,400 voters) to force a referendum.
affected_projects: 80 Merritt Blvd. (former Nasdaq data center, 15 MW capacity) -- explicitly excluded from the moratorium's scope as an existing-facility modernization, not a new data center; First Selectman Vicki Tesoro reported the operator (365 Data Centers/Aphorio Carter) agreed to no increase in electrical draw, noise, or water use, and no expansion of the building footprint, as part of ongoing negotiations.
outcome: 2-year moratorium on new data center establishment/development adopted unanimously; does not reach the town's existing (and currently most active) data center project, which continues as a modernization outside the moratorium's scope.

date_enacted: 2026-06-08, per City Council meeting minutes
duration: 1 year
legal_basis: City Council resolution requiring a 1-year moratorium on the development of data centers, requested by Mayor Dorinda Borer
trigger: Not detailed beyond the mayor's request in captured minutes
current_status: Adopted unanimously; not independently re-checked past 2026-06-08
affected_projects: Not identified in captured minutes
outcome: Council unanimously approved a 1-year moratorium on data center development

duration: 18 months from the ordinance's effective date, as drafted; the Council may extend by ordinance upon findings that additional study remains necessary. Not yet adopted as of 2026-09-23.
legal_basis: Draft ordinance amending the Dover Code to add a 'Large Energy Use Facility' moratorium, sponsored by Councilwoman Donyale Hall and Councilman David Anderson; heard by the Council Committee of the Whole (Legislative, Finance and Administration Committee) on 2026-09-15, which recommended forwarding it to full Council and the Planning Commission for review. No ordinance number assigned; the city's official Ordinances/Resolutions register lists nothing past Ordinance 2026-13 (adopted 2026-08-10) as of 2026-09-23.
trigger: Multiple inquiries about 'Large Energy Use Facilities' (data centers meeting defined MW/load thresholds); city wants time to study electrical capacity, ratepayer cost allocation, infrastructure, land use, environmental standards, and economic impact before adopting permanent regulations
current_status: Pending as of 2026-09-23. The draft ordinance would immediately suspend the City's acceptance, processing, review, approval, and issuance of permits, site plan approvals, conditional-use approvals, rezonings, subdivision approvals, building permits, utility service agreements, and certificates of occupancy for any new 'Large Energy Use Facility' (a facility using 75+ MW at 85%+ load factor, 100+ MW instantaneous demand, or 30+ MW and NAICS 518210) for 18 months, with exemptions for government/hospital/university/public-safety/clean-hydrogen facilities and small expansions. First proposed publicly in August 2026 (a City Council committee voted unanimously to advance a draft to full Council); the Council Committee of the Whole heard the finalized ordinance text on 2026-09-15 and recommended it go to full Council and the Planning Commission, but no first or final reading before full Council, and no ordinance number, had been recorded as of 2026-09-23. A sponsor's public social-media post described the proposal as a 24-month moratorium, which conflicts with the 18-month term stated in the drafted ordinance text reviewed here; the ordinance text is treated as authoritative.
affected_projects: None named; city officials said they have been approached about at least one small-to-medium data center project but declined to identify it.

date_enacted: Approved by the Board of County Commissioners 2026-07-07 (reported 2026-07-08).
duration: Six-month moratorium on data centers requiring 5 MW of power or more in unincorporated Bay County, while staff reviews and updates land development regulations; may be extended another six months if permanent rules are not ready.
legal_basis: Bay County Board of County Commissioners ordinance (specific ordinance number not located in reviewed sources); adopted 2026-07-07.
trigger: Months of public discussion and comment on proposed AI data centers in unincorporated Bay County.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; six-month pause on data centers of 5 MW or more, set to run roughly through early January 2027, while planning staff update land development regulations.
outcome: Six-month moratorium adopted; permanent regulations expected before it expires, or a further six-month extension possible.

date_enacted: Adopted 2026-05-26 by the Board of County Commissioners at a public hearing, 5-0 vote; staff had been directed on 2026-05-12 to prepare the ordinance for that meeting.
duration: In effect for 12 months from its effective date or until related county regulations take effect, whichever occurs first.
legal_basis: Citrus County Ordinance No. 2026-02
trigger: County-initiated pause pending development of local data-center regulations; more than 40 public speakers attended the May 26 hearing.
current_status: Active moratorium halting construction/expansion approvals, building permits, development orders, and rezonings for data center facilities in unincorporated Citrus County.

date_enacted: Adopted 2026-06-23 by the Board of County Commissioners, 4-1 vote, following a first hearing 2026-06-09.
duration: One-year moratorium in unincorporated Clay County.
legal_basis: Clay County ordinance (ordinance number not located in reviewed sources); the official agenda title describes the measure as pausing acceptance, review, or approval of applications for land-use amendments to the Clay County 2045 Comprehensive Plan related to data-center facilities.
trigger: More than an hour of public testimony at the final hearing.
current_status: Active; the official scope is narrower (comprehensive-plan land-use amendments) than some news descriptions of a blanket permit freeze, and that narrower scope should be preferred.

date_enacted: Commissioners approved the moratorium unanimously (4-0, one commissioner recused) 2026-07-28 (Tuesday).
duration: One-year moratorium on new data-center applications in DeSoto County; explicitly does not apply to rezoning applications already pending for DCIP Group's 800-plus-acre data-center project (which can continue to move forward).
legal_basis: DeSoto County Board of County Commissioners ordinance (specific ordinance number not located in reviewed sources); adopted 2026-07-28.
trigger: Intense public opposition to DCIP Group's proposed data-center campus (initially a 34-acre rezoning at a decommissioned power plant, since expanded with an 800-plus-acre rezoning request and stated intent to build on up to 1,300 acres).
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; one-year moratorium adopted 2026-07-28, with DCIP Group's pending rezoning applications exempted from its coverage.
affected_projects: DCIP Group data-center campus (decommissioned power-plant site; pending rezoning of 800+ additional acres; company has said it hopes to build more than a dozen facilities across roughly 1,300 acres) -- exempted from the moratorium.
outcome: One-year moratorium adopted, county attorney limited scope to one year and excluded pending applications rather than following the Planning Commission's recommendation of a two-year moratorium covering the DCIP Group applications.

date_enacted: Adopted on second reading by the Board of County Commissioners 2026-08-03 (Monday), unanimous.
duration: One-year moratorium on new data center development in unincorporated Flagler County while the county researches the industry and develops zoning/land development regulations. Amended before final passage to remove the 'large-scale'/'large load customer facility' qualifiers so the pause applies to all data centers, not only large ones.
legal_basis: Flagler County ordinance (adopted on second reading 2026-08-03; specific ordinance number not located in reviewed sources).
trigger: Months of discussion about the rapid growth of the data-center industry and resident concerns about impacts on electrical infrastructure, water, noise, and land use.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; one-year moratorium applying only to unincorporated Flagler County (does not affect projects within municipal boundaries such as Palm Coast).
outcome: One-year moratorium adopted on second reading, broadened at final passage to cover all data centers rather than only large-scale ones.

date_enacted: Commissioners voted unanimously to approve the moratorium 2026-07-15 (Wednesday morning), after directing staff in June to prepare it.
duration: One-year moratorium on large-scale AI data center proposals, while commissioners consider a permanent ban.
legal_basis: Franklin County Board of County Commissioners ordinance (specific ordinance number not located in reviewed sources); adopted 2026-07-15.
trigger: Precautionary; more than one commissioner stated an eventual goal of a permanent ban.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; one-year moratorium on large-scale AI data center proposals adopted 2026-07-15.
outcome: One-year moratorium adopted unanimously.

date_enacted: Adopted 2026-06-23 at second public hearing (first hearing 2026-06-02); Florida Department of State acknowledged filing 2026-06-24.
duration: 365-day moratorium on development orders and permits for data centers in unincorporated Hernando County, subject to exemptions and prospective-application provisions; can end early if permanent regulations take effect, and can be extended once for no more than 120 days.
legal_basis: Hernando County Ordinance 2026-15
current_status: Active 365-day moratorium; filed with the Florida Department of State 2026-06-24.

date_enacted: Board of County Commissioners voted unanimously to adopt the ordinance 2026-09-09 (Tuesday).
duration: 90-day pause on accepting any applications for large-scale data centers in unincorporated Lake County, to give commissioners time to create new zoning and development regulations (including a possible conditional-use-permit requirement).
legal_basis: Lake County ordinance citing Senate Bill 484 local authority (specific ordinance number not located in reviewed sources); adopted 2026-09-09.
trigger: Regulatory gap; county wants a conditional-use-permit process so a data center is not a guaranteed right.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; 90-day pause adopted 2026-09-09, running to approximately early December 2026.
outcome: 90-day moratorium adopted, a shorter and later instrument than the one-year moratorium the Board had directed staff to draft in late June.

date_enacted: 2026-08-03, City Commission adopted Ordinance No. 26-018 by a 4-3 vote.
duration: One year from 2026-08-03, unless amended or repealed sooner. Covers new data centers and large-load customers with anticipated peak demand of 50 MW or more while the City reviews its planning and land-development rules.
legal_basis: City of Lakeland Ordinance No. 26-018, adopted 2026-08-03 by a 4-3 vote
trigger: Followed community opposition to Project Swan, a proposed approximately 600,000-square-foot data center.
current_status: Active as of 2026-08-19. The City Commission adopted Ordinance No. 26-018 4-3 on 2026-08-03, pausing acceptance, processing, review, and approval of covered applications for one year.
affected_projects: Project Swan (proposed approximately 600,000 sq ft data center; Kimley-Horn on behalf of Ryan Companies U.S., Inc.)
outcome: Ordinance No. 26-018 is effective immediately and pauses new covered applications while the City considers permanent rules.

date_enacted: Commissioners directed staff in July 2026 to pursue an ordinance; the proposed ordinance passed its first of two required public hearings unanimously 2026-09-15. The second and final public hearing/vote is scheduled for 2026-10-13 and had not occurred as of this research date.
duration: Proposed 18-month moratorium on large-load customer facilities, including large-scale data centers, in unincorporated Leon County, to give staff time to study impacts on electricity/water supplies, utility rates, the environment, and surrounding communities and to develop regulations; staff plans to report findings by September 2027.
legal_basis: Proposed Leon County ordinance (first reading passed 2026-09-15; not yet adopted).
trigger: Proposal originated with Commission Chairman Christian Caban after SB 484 took effect 2026-07-01; county code and the Tallahassee-Leon County 2050 Comprehensive Plan lack provisions addressing large-load customers/data centers.
current_status: Pending as of 2026-09-23; first reading passed unanimously 2026-09-15, with the second and final public hearing scheduled for 2026-10-13. County staff report no approved or pending large-scale data-center applications in unincorporated Leon County as of this filing.
outcome: First reading passed unanimously; final adoption pending as of 2026-09-23.

date_enacted: Adopted 2026-06-23 by City Commission.
duration: Interim pause on accepting, processing, reviewing, or acting on data-center applications, lasting until the earlier of final action on a separate proposed one-year moratorium ordinance or sixty days after this resolution's adoption (on or about 2026-08-22).
legal_basis: City of Lynn Haven Resolution 2026-06-561
trigger: Adopted while a separate one-year moratorium ordinance (staff directed to draft it on 2026-06-09) proceeded through the adoption process; this resolution is a distinct interim instrument from that still-pending ordinance.
current_status: Expired 2026-08-22; Resolution 2026-06-561 provided by its own terms that it would remain in effect only until the earlier of (a) City Commission adoption of the separate 'Moratorium Ordinance,' (b) the Commission formally declining to adopt it, or (c) 60 days from the resolution's 2026-06-23 adoption. Review of the City's official agenda/minutes packets for every City Commission meeting from 2026-07-14 through 2026-09-22 (plus special meetings 2026-09-16 and 2026-09-21) found no Data Center/AI Data Center Moratorium Ordinance ever placed on an agenda for either reading, and no news coverage of its adoption, decline, or extension. The 60-day clock therefore ran out on 2026-08-22 without the city having adopted, declined, or extended the pause.

date_enacted: Board of County Commissioners voted unanimously 2026-07-22.
duration: One-year moratorium on construction and permitting of large-scale data centers while the county develops possible regulations.
legal_basis: Madison County ordinance (signed ordinance, ordinance number, effective date, and exact expiration date not located in reviewed sources).
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Confirmed via the county's local newspaper of record (Greene Publishing / Madison County Carrier) and a Suwannee Riverkeeper (WWALS) report that tracked the ordinance through both readings: first reading 2026-07-08, second reading and 4-0 final adoption 2026-07-22, imposing a one-year moratorium on construction and permitting of large-scale data center facilities. No subsequent extension, repeal, or replacement found. [VERIFY instrument/ordinance number: the enacted ordinance's assigned number was still not located in a signed county document as of 2026-09-23]

date_enacted: Commissioners directed staff to draft the ordinance 2026-07-28; the Board of County Commissioners applied the Pending Ordinance Doctrine and adopted Ordinance No. 26-42 on 2026-09-22 (first noticed for public hearing 2026-09-04; Planning Commission review 2026-09-17).
duration: Twelve-month moratorium on submission and acceptance of applications for building permits, site plans, development orders, development agreements, special permit uses, rezonings, and comprehensive plan amendments related to 'Data Center Facilities' in unincorporated Manatee County, or until repealed, whichever occurs first; may be extended by Board resolution.
legal_basis: Manatee County Ordinance No. 26-42
trigger: SB 484 (effective 2026-07-01) established local authority over large-load customers; county's land development code and comprehensive plan do not adequately address data centers.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23 (adopted the day before); twelve-month moratorium running through approximately 2027-09-22.
outcome: Twelve-month moratorium ordinance (No. 26-42) adopted.

date_enacted: Board of County Commissioners voted 4-1 on the substantive motion, then 5-0 on a subsequent procedural vote to adopt the ordinance, at a public hearing 2026-09-15/16 (hearing held 2026-09-15 at the McPherson Governmental Campus; reported 2026-09-16).
duration: 12-month (365-day) moratorium on accepting or processing applications for major commercial data centers, AI processing hubs, and cryptocurrency-mining operations, applying to development permits, site plans, rezonings, and conditional-use permits; exempts smaller facilities using under 50 megawatts, which may still proceed through the county's standard Special Use Permit process.
legal_basis: Marion County Board of County Commissioners ordinance (specific ordinance number not located in reviewed sources); adopted 2026-09-15.
trigger: Concerns over water consumption from the Floridan Aquifer (including Outstanding Florida Springs Silver Springs and Rainbow Springs), power-grid strain, noise, and county staff's stated lack of readiness/criteria to evaluate large data-center applications; balanced against a proposed roughly $10 billion facility that proponents said could generate significant tax revenue and jobs.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; 12-month moratorium adopted 2026-09-15, with an exemption for facilities under 50 MW that can still apply via Special Use Permit.
affected_projects: An unnamed proposed data-center facility reported by proponents at the hearing as a roughly $10 billion project that could generate about $155 million in tax revenue.
outcome: 12-month moratorium adopted (4-1 substantive vote; 5-0 procedural adoption vote), with exemptions for sub-50-MW facilities that drew a dissenting vote from Commissioner Kathy Bryant, who opposed the carve-out.

date_enacted: Adopted on final hearing 2026-06-08 by the Nassau County Board of County Commissioners (motion by Commissioner Gray, seconded by Commissioner Farmer, approved); first reading was 2026-05-11, following direction to draft on 2026-04-13.
duration: 12 months from the effective date, or until an ordinance amending the Comprehensive Plan, Land Development Regulations, and/or Code of Ordinances relating to Data Center Facilities takes effect, whichever occurs first (Ordinance 2026-044, Section 6). Effective date is upon filing with the Florida Secretary of State per s. 125.66.
legal_basis: Nassau County Ordinance No. 2026-044, "Imposing a Temporary Moratorium on the Acceptance, Review, or Approval of Applications for Development Permits, Development Orders, Rezoning, or Site Plans Related to Data Centers, Data Processing Facilities, Data Mining or Cryptocurrency Mining Operations ... Within Unincorporated Nassau County, Florida."
trigger: Board directed staff to draft the moratorium in April 2026 to allow time to study and adopt comprehensive-plan and land-development-code provisions for data centers before accepting further applications; a companion resolution (2026-102) created a Fact-Finding Committee on Data Center Development that met repeatedly through June 2026.
current_status: Active as of 2026-07-31. Checked the June 22, July 13, and July 27, 2026 BOCC agendas; no repeal, amendment, or extension item found. Applies only to unincorporated Nassau County.
affected_projects: No specific pending project named in the ordinance itself; adopted preemptively alongside the Fact-Finding Committee on Data Center Development.
outcome: Ordinance adopted on final hearing 2026-06-08; moratorium in effect for up to 12 months or until permanent Data Center Facility regulations are adopted, whichever is sooner.

date_enacted: City Commission voted 4-1 to advance the ordinance on first reading 2026-09-08 (after a nearly seven-hour public hearing beginning 2026-08-31); adopted on second and final reading by a 3-2 vote 2026-09-22 (Commissioners Stokes, Langdon and Mayor Emrich in favor; Commissioners Petrow and Duval against).
duration: 18-month moratorium on the acceptance and approval of new data-center applications. As finally adopted, the ordinance excludes (does not apply to) the roughly 896,000-square-foot data-center facility already proposed for the Yorkshire-area 'Deep Park' development: staff may still accept, process and review that application, but the city cannot approve it without a City Commission vote. The ordinance also allows any developer to request an 'extraordinary hardship' exception (e.g., permits already issued, substantial expenditure already made), decided case-by-case by the Commission.
legal_basis: City of North Port ordinance (specific ordinance number not located in reviewed sources); adopted on second/final reading 2026-09-22.
trigger: A roughly 896,000 sq ft ('Deep Park') data-center application, part of a larger 282-acre mixed-use development, submitted 2026-07-20 after a non-disclosure agreement (entered August 2025) expired; hundreds of residents packed multiple public hearings (2026-08-31 and 2026-09-22) in opposition, citing water, noise, and infrastructure concerns.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23 (adopted the day before, 3-2); 18-month moratorium on new data-center applications, but the already-pending ~896,000 sq ft Deep Park data-center application is excluded from the pause (city staff may still process it; Commission approval is still required) rather than being retroactively swept in.
affected_projects: The 'Deep Park' data-center proposal: roughly 896,000 sq ft of buildings (about 123,200 sq ft of office space) on land near Yorkshire Street/Oleander Drive, part of a broader 282-acre 'employment epicenter' development; excluded from the moratorium's coverage as finally adopted.
outcome: 18-month moratorium adopted 3-2 on second/final reading 2026-09-22; the pending Deep Park application was excluded from coverage after the city attorney warned that including it could expose the city to litigation.

date_enacted: Board of County Commissioners approved zoning in progress effective 2026-07-07 and directed staff to prepare a formal moratorium ordinance.
duration: Interim administrative freeze: staff directed not to accept new large-load-customer data center applications until a formal ordinance is presented for adoption. The contemplated formal ordinance would run until the earlier of one year after its adoption or the enactment of permanent regulations.
legal_basis: Board of County Commissioners zoning-in-progress directive, 2026-07-07 (formal ordinance not yet adopted as of the reviewed sources)
trigger: Followed opposition to Project Tango and other large-load data center proposals.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. The July 7 interim intake freeze remains in force. The formal one-year moratorium ordinance (defining a 'large-scale' facility at 50 MW+ peak demand, with site-wide load aggregation to prevent parcel-splitting, and carve-outs for hurricane-damaged parcels) passed first reading unanimously 7-0 on 2026-08-27; the Board is scheduled to hold the second and final public hearing and possible formal adoption on 2026-09-24 (i.e., the day after this research date), so the ordinance had not yet been finally adopted as of 2026-09-23. [VERIFY instrument number for the July 7 interim zoning-in-progress directive; still not located in an official numbered document]
affected_projects: Project Tango (Central Park Commerce Center data center expansion)

date_enacted: Adopted on second/final reading by the City Commission 2026-09-23 (Ordinance 3313); first public hearing held 2026-09-08.
duration: One-year moratorium on new data center proposals, giving city staff 12 months to study impacts and develop permanent zoning rules; does not apply to existing facilities or routine maintenance.
legal_basis: City of Panama City Ordinance 3313
trigger: Regulatory-gap/precautionary; part of a wave of Bay County-area moratoria.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23 (adopted the same day); one-year pause on new large-scale data center proposals.
outcome: One-year moratorium adopted on second reading.

date_enacted: Commissioners unanimously approved 2026-07-14, following a Planning Commission recommendation 2026-06-11 and a first BOCC hearing 2026-06-16.
duration: One-year moratorium pausing covered development approvals for server or computer rooms exceeding 2.5 MW in unincorporated Pasco County while the county studies definitions and environmental, utility, and financial impacts.
legal_basis: Pasco County ordinance (signed ordinance number and exact expiration date not located in reviewed sources).
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Confirmed via WUSF (public radio) and the county's own pre-adoption ordinance text (agenda packet), which sets a 12-month duration 'or until such time as repealed by the Board, whichever occurs first.' No extension, repeal, or replacement found through 2026-09-23.

date_enacted: First reading passed 7-0 on 2026-07-16; adopted on second and final reading by a 7-0 vote at the 2026-08-13 City Council Regular Meeting as Ordinance No. 11-26 (agenda item 'Proposed Ordinance No. 13-26').
duration: Proposed one-year moratorium on city approvals for data centers and other large-load-customer facilities with anticipated monthly peak demand of at least 50 MW; would take effect five business days after final adoption.
legal_basis: City of Pensacola Ordinance No. 11-26 (introduced as Proposed Ordinance No. 13-26; adopted 2026-08-13 on second reading, 7-0)

date_enacted: Placed on first reading 2026-07-21; adopted unanimously at the 2026-08-11 public hearing as Ordinance 2026-22.

The pause ends at the earlier of a land development code amendment or 12 months (i.e. on or about 2026-08-11-2027).

current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Confirmed via the county's own BOCC Special Rezoning Meeting agenda (2026-07-23) and the Santa Rosa Press Gazette (local paper of record), both corroborating the PNJ reporting that the ordinance was adopted at the 2026-07-23 special meeting. [VERIFY instrument/ordinance number: still not located in a signed county document as of 2026-09-23]

date_enacted: Board of County Commissioners voted unanimously to approve the moratorium 2026-08-20 (Thursday), following a public hearing.
duration: One-year moratorium on data-center development in unincorporated Washington County (municipalities Chipley, Wausau, and Caryville are not covered, as they control their own development). A facility is defined as a data center if more than 5% of a building's gross floor area is used for computer systems/hardware/racks, in addition to an electrical-usage threshold, with anti-fragmentation language to prevent splitting a project across smaller buildings. May be extended by a further ordinance if permanent regulations are not ready in time.
legal_basis: Washington County ordinance (specific ordinance number not located in reviewed sources); adopted 2026-08-20.
trigger: Regulatory gap; county comprehensive plan and land development code do not adequately address data-center infrastructure and public-safety impacts.

legal_basis: Ordinance No. O-2526-70 (City of Norman); applies to new applications for data center facilities using evaporative cooling projected to consume more than 250,000 gallons of potable water per day; applications filed before the ordinance's effective date are outside its stated scope
trigger: Water consumption concerns from evaporative-cooling data centers
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; runs through June 9, 2027 or the effective date of new data-center zoning regulations, whichever is earlier, per Ordinance No. O-2526-70. No amendment, extension, or repeal was found in city records or news coverage through 2026-09-23.

duration: Until 2026-12-31, or earlier if data center zoning amendments are adopted
legal_basis: Ordinance No. 28,071 (City of Oklahoma City), introduced, read, and passed with emergency on 2026-04-21 (Council Agenda Item XI.U), signed by the Mayor the same day; exempts pending rezoning applications PUD-2105 and PUD-2124. Amended 2026-05-19 by a 7-2 Council vote (per a City Manager memo amending Ordinance No. 28,071, adding a Section 7 definition limiting the moratorium to data centers with net-new electrical loads greater than 75 MW and a further exemption for the proposed project at 7725 N. Reno Ave. conditioned on potable-water use being limited to domestic/irrigation/fire-protection purposes); the specific ordinance number assigned to the May 19, 2026 amendment itself was not located.
trigger: First large data center rezoning requests; no specific zoning use unit or regulations for data centers; concerns about water, electricity, noise, infrastructure, and other public impacts
current_status: Active, as amended, as of 2026-09-23; runs through Dec. 31, 2026 or the effective date of new data-center zoning-code amendments, whichever is earlier (Ordinance No. 28,071, Section 4). The May 19, 2026 amendment (7-2 vote) limited the moratorium to data centers with net-new electrical loads over 75 MW and added exemptions for the Expand Energy campus facility (serving Cerebras AI) and a facility at 7725 N. Reno Ave. No comprehensive data-center zoning use-unit had been adopted as of 2026-09-23 in any source reviewed in this pass, so the moratorium (as amended) remains in force; no further amendment or repeal was found.
affected_projects: New applications for rezoning requests and permits, including building permits, for data center construction, expansion, or use; two pending rezoning requests are exempted
outcome: City is using the pause to evaluate impacts and draft zoning code amendments for data centers

duration: Until 2026-12-31, or earlier if data center regulations are adopted
legal_basis: Resolution 2026-04-01
trigger: Proposed conversion of an abandoned warehouse near Indian Camp Elementary School into an 8-10 MW AI data center; utility capacity, water, school proximity, property values, and community-impact concerns
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; runs through Dec. 31, 2026 or earlier adoption of data-center regulations. The pause halted the proposed Buckley Bros Holdings conversion of a vacant 200,000-sq-ft carpet mill into an 8-10 MW AI data center; as of an Aug. 31, 2026 status check, 'no progress on the project can begin... until January 2027' and no relocation announcement had been made. No amendment, extension, or repeal was found in news coverage through 2026-09-23.
affected_projects: All city actions that would advance data center development in Pawhuska
outcome: City will gather information and develop zoning, permitting, and performance-standard recommendations

duration: Indefinite by design, not merely undisclosed. Per KGOU reporting (June 25, 2026), the resolution's author, Rev. Chebon Kernell, originally drafted a ban on data-center discussions/inquiries/development, but 'that proposal turned into an indefinite moratorium at the suggestion of another council member.' The resolution's own phrase 'the moratorium period' (as quoted by Native News Online) therefore refers to an open-ended condition rather than a fixed numeric term that simply has not been published. The full resolution text remains unposted on sno-nsn.gov.
legal_basis: General Council of the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma, Tribal Resolution TR 2026-38, 'A Verbal Resolution... Implementing a Moratorium on the Advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence Technology and Hyperscale Data Center Development within the Jurisdiction of the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma,' passed and approved at Mekusukey Mission on March 7, 2026 by a vote of 24 Yes, 0 No, 0 Abstaining (quorum of 15 present).
trigger: Startup approach seeking an NDA and letter of intent to develop a data center on Seminole lands; environmental, water, sovereignty, and community-health concerns
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. TR 2026-38 bars 'any inquiries, discussions, and/or developments concerning any entity seeking to develop a data center of any size within the Seminole Nation... during the moratorium period,' with no stated end date (open-ended by design, per KGOU/KOSU reporting on the resolution's drafting history). Multiple independent sources through Aug. 20, 2026 (KOSU, Turtle Talk blog, Current Tribal Law) continue to describe the moratorium as in force, with no rescission, amendment, or replacement framework identified as of 2026-09-23. No Tribal Council minutes confirming continued force were located on the Seminole Nation's own website in this pass either.
affected_projects: Any inquiries, discussions, or developments concerning data centers of any size within the Seminole Nation during the moratorium period
outcome: Moratorium adopted before project approval; permanent replacement framework not identified

date_enacted: 2026-08-17 (Monday), Shawnee City Commission, unanimous 7-0 vote; resolution sponsored by Commissioner Chris Odneal
duration: From adoption through December 31, 2027
legal_basis: Shawnee City Commission resolution (specific resolution/instrument number not located in captured coverage), sponsored by Commissioner Chris Odneal, freezing new data center applications through Dec. 31, 2027
trigger: Preemptive pause to allow city staff to study how large-scale data centers might strain local power and water systems, and to update city regulations, before accepting new proposals; city staff had initially estimated a 90-day study period would suffice, but Commissioners opted for a longer runway through the end of 2027. Discussions ahead of the vote also touched on land-use questions involving the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, whose tribal headquarters are in Shawnee.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Moratorium adopted Aug. 17, 2026 on a unanimous 7-0 vote, effective immediately, freezing new data-center applications through Dec. 31, 2027; does not affect any data center projects already operating or under construction in Shawnee. Staff committed to reporting findings within 90 days of adoption.
affected_projects: None named; no current applications were pending at adoption. Applies only to new applications going forward, not to any existing operating or under-construction projects.
outcome: Shawnee City Commission adopted a moratorium freezing new data center applications through the end of 2027, directing staff to study power and water impacts and update city regulations before the pause lifts.

date_enacted: 2026-03-25 (unanimous Council vote; reported by Oklahoma Energy Today and Tulsa Flyer; ordinance text included emergency clause requiring immediate effectiveness, so adoption and effective dates coincide)
duration: Through 2026-12-31, or earlier if data center zoning amendments are adopted
legal_basis: Tulsa City Council File/Ordinance No. 26-196 (final substitute version "26-196-3"), reviewed by the Urban Development committee and Council on 2026-03-11 and adopted by the Budget/Special Projects committee and Council on 2026-03-25. A redlined draft of the ordinance (marked 'JCB 3/25/26') shows the bill's caption and Section 4 term were amended from a flat '365-DAY' moratorium to a fixed expiration of 'December 31, 2026, or on the effective date of an ordinance amending data center regulations..., whichever is earlier'; the amendment also renumbered sections to add a Section 4 '60-DAY REPORTS' requirement for the Planning Office. This resolves the tension between the city's caption text and Tulsa Flyer's '9 months' reporting: the final adopted term is the Dec. 31, 2026 calendar date, not a literal 365-day count from adoption.
trigger: Re-evaluation of Tulsa's 2024 classification of data centers as low-impact manufacturing and industry; concern that large-scale data centers may have off-site impacts
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; runs through Dec. 31, 2026 (the term as actually adopted, notwithstanding the ordinance's '365-day' caption -- see legal_basis) or the effective date of new data-center zoning regulations, whichever is earlier. An Aug. 24, 2026 Tulsa Flyer report confirms the moratorium 'went into effect March 25 and expires Dec. 31,' that the Planning Office's first 60-day report has been produced and recommends reclassifying data centers by square footage and widening setbacks from 250 to 1,500 feet, and that final zoning recommendations are due to Council in November 2026, after which Council could adopt them or extend the moratorium. No extension or repeal had occurred as of 2026-09-23.
affected_projects: New building permits for data center use in Tulsa; Project Anthem Phase 1 and one pending Phase 2 zoning case are exempted
outcome: Planning Office must report to Council approximately every 60 days on zoning-code review and recommendations

date_enacted: 2026-07-27 (City Council adopted signed Resolution No. 2932 at a special meeting, effective immediately)
duration: 120 days unless extended or repealed, with mandatory council review before expiration
legal_basis: Resolution No. 2932, adopted by the Hillsboro City Council at a special meeting on July 27, 2026
trigger: City sought time to study data center and battery storage impacts and develop code amendments; contemporaneous coverage described Hillsboro as the first Oregon city to adopt a data center land-use moratorium
current_status: Active as of the July 31, 2026 research date. Effective immediately upon adoption, the resolution bars submission, acceptance, processing, or approval of new land-use applications for new or expanded data centers or battery energy storage systems as primary uses. Applications already under review are not affected. Runs 120 days (to approximately 2026-11-24) absent extension or repeal, with council review required before expiration.
affected_projects: New or expanded stand-alone data center or battery energy storage system land-use applications submitted after July 27, 2026; does not affect applications already under review.
outcome: Enacted moratorium on new data center and battery storage land-use applications while the city studies impacts and develops code amendments.

The Board of Commissioners voted unanimously on approximately 2026-08-04/08-05 to begin the formal process for a moratorium; Oregon law requires 45 days' notice to the Department of Land Conservation and Development before a public hearing on the proposed moratorium can be held. As of a September 15, 2026 news report, Clackamas County was still described as merely 'considering' a moratorium (alongside Salem, which adopted its own that month); no report of a final Board vote to adopt the moratorium was found as of 2026-09-23.

current_status: Pending as of 2026-09-23. No data center land-use application had been filed in the county as of this pass.
