date_enacted: 2026-09-21 (City Council unanimous vote at a special session)
duration: 120 days from adoption (2026-09-21 to 2027-01-19); Oregon law allows extensions of up to 300 additional days with additional findings.
legal_basis: Moratorium ordinance adopted by the Salem City Council on 2026-09-21, following an August 3, 2026 council vote to move forward with the moratorium and a resolution to begin updating zoning/land-use code; required 45-day notice to the Oregon Department of Land Conservation and Development preceded formal adoption.
trigger: specific_project
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Moratorium halts construction of all data centers (as a primary use) and accessory data centers with facility capacity greater than 2 megawatts, effective 2026-09-21 through 2027-01-19. City Attorney Dan Atchison based the moratorium on a compelling need to prevent public harm, citing the city's water supply risk from the impending deep drawdown of the Detroit Reservoir (serving roughly 220,000 water customers). The moratorium does not block Verrus's already-filed land use application for a 600,000-square-foot data center (filed late July 2026, before the moratorium), since Oregon law generally requires applications to be reviewed under rules in effect when filed, but the city attorney confirmed construction itself can be prohibited during the moratorium.
affected_projects: Verrus Group filed a land use application in late July 2026 for a roughly 600,000-square-foot data center in Salem; the application proceeds under pre-moratorium review rules, but the moratorium bars construction while it is in effect.
outcome: City Council unanimously adopted a 120-day moratorium halting data center construction while the city develops permanent zoning and land-use regulations.

date_enacted: 2026-09-14 (City Council unanimous 6-0 vote)
duration: 120 days from adoption (2026-09-14 to 2027-01-12); the City Manager stated the council could extend it to up to six months total.
legal_basis: Moratorium ordinance adopted by the Woodburn City Council on 2026-09-14; the city filed the required 45-day notice of intent to consider a moratorium with the Oregon Department of Land Conservation and Development on 2026-07-30 before the council could act.
trigger: specific_project
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Moratorium prevents city planning staff from considering any new data center land-use application, effective 2026-09-14 through 2027-01-12. Adopted after the city learned that data center developer Verrus (which had separately applied to build in Salem, where its application drew significant public resistance) was exploring development of a data center on a 237-acre privately owned Southwest Industrial Reserve Area parcel brought into Woodburn's urban growth boundary in 2025; Woodburn had not received a formal application as of adoption. The city separately adopted an ordinance in June 2026 designating data centers as a conditional use in that industrial reserve area, and has hired a consultant (Thomas Consulting Group) to help review and potentially revise its development code for data centers.
affected_projects: No formal application received; city staff learned that data center developer Verrus was exploring a site 'in or near Woodburn,' including the 237-acre Southwest Industrial Reserve Area.
outcome: City Council unanimously adopted a 120-day moratorium on considering new data center applications while the city reviews and potentially revises its development code.

date_enacted: 2026-07-13, Adams Township Board of Supervisors, unanimous resolution formalizing a June 22, 2026 motion to establish the moratorium (Butler County)
duration: 180 days from the July 13, 2026 resolution (following the June 22, 2026 motion) to draft a curative amendment addressing six business types not covered by current zoning: data centers, power generation plants, large-scale and accessory solar power systems, last-mile fulfillment centers, micro-warehouses, and dispensaries.
legal_basis: Adams Township Board of Supervisors resolution (a follow-up to the June 22, 2026 motion), invoking the municipal curative amendment process under the PA Municipalities Planning Code and declaring the zoning ordinance's exclusion of the six business types 'does not bear a substantial relationship to the public health, safety or morals' of residents, and that a sweeping ban 'cannot pass constitutional muster' and is therefore invalid (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed).
trigger: Regulatory gap: current zoning ordinance does not address data centers, power generation plants, large-scale/accessory solar, last-mile fulfillment centers, micro-warehouses, or dispensaries, allowing any of them to be built anywhere in the township. Board Chairman Russell Ford emphasized the action was preemptive, not prompted by any pending application.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its computed 180-day expiry (~2027-01-09). Adopted via a unanimous June 22, 2026 motion and formalized by resolution at the July 13, 2026 meeting, the moratorium pauses applications for six business types (data centers, power generation plants, large-scale/accessory solar, last-mile fulfillment centers, micro-warehouses, dispensaries) while the township prepares a curative amendment to correct the declared invalidity. No news of an extension, adoption of the amendment, or repeal was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
affected_projects: None named; officials stated the moratorium was preemptive and not prompted by any pending application for any of the six covered business types.
outcome: Adams Township Board of Supervisors adopted a 180-day moratorium (via a June 22, 2026 motion, formalized by resolution on July 13, 2026) on six business types including data centers and large-scale solar, to allow time to draft a curative amendment to the zoning ordinance.

date_enacted: Township Council adopted a curative-amendment resolution by a 5-0 vote on 2026-06-08.
duration: 180-day municipal curative-amendment period after declaring portions of the zoning ordinance substantively invalid as to data centers, solar energy, and wind energy. Official minutes describe the protected period as a 180-day moratorium.
legal_basis: Township Council resolution, Municipal Curative Amendment (Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code Section 609.2)
trigger: Zoning ordinance lacked provisions for data centers, solar energy, and wind energy.
current_status: Active as of 2026-07-31; 180-day curative-amendment period from 2026-06-08. No data center application was pending at adoption.

date_enacted: Borough Council reportedly voted unanimously on 2026-06-16 for a 180-day moratorium.
duration: 180-day moratorium on data center development; also bars data centers from using borough water during the pause.
legal_basis: Confirmed via three independent contemporaneous news reports (WPSU, The Courier-Express/Jeffersonian Democrat, and explorejeffersonpa.com/EYT) that the moratorium was adopted as a Borough Council motion -- made by Second Vice-President Randy Bartley during the property committee's report at the June 16, 2026 regular meeting -- rather than as a separately numbered ordinance or resolution. The Courier-Express: 'The moratorium was approved during a report by the property committee regarding some rezoning in the borough. The motion was made by Randy Bartley... The motion passed unanimously.' No ordinance or resolution number exists for this action because it was adopted by motion.
trigger: Water-resource concerns tied to potential nearby data center projects; no formal application was pending.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its computed 180-day expiry (~2026-12-13/14). Adopted by unanimous Borough Council motion on 2026-06-16, pausing data center development in the borough and barring data centers from using Brookville's municipal water system (which also serves Corsica, Pinecreek Elementary School, and the Jefferson County Fairgrounds outside the borough). The action was prompted by unofficial word of two possible nearby data center projects -- one in Pine Creek Township, one in Rose Township -- that officials estimated could together require about 2.4 million gallons of water per day; no formal application had been filed for either as of adoption. No news of an extension, permanent ordinance, or repeal was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.

date_enacted: 2026-08-12, Buffalo Township Board of Supervisors, regular meeting vote creating a municipal curative amendment (Butler County)
duration: 180 days from adoption to draft and adopt zoning standards for data centers; effectively bars new data-center project proposals during that window by preempting a landowner-initiated curative amendment.
legal_basis: Buffalo Township municipal curative amendment under PA Municipalities Planning Code Section 609.2 (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed)
trigger: Regulatory gap: township zoning ordinance does not address data centers; adopted proactively -- following similar action in other Butler County townships (Adams, Center, Lancaster) -- specifically to prevent a developer from forcing the issue via a landowner curative amendment.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. 180-day municipal curative amendment adopted 2026-08-12, giving the township until approximately 2027-02-08 to draft and adopt data-center zoning standards; effectively functions as a moratorium on new data-center proposals during that period, per township solicitor Brian Farrington ('I don't want to call it a moratorium, but effectively, it is').
affected_projects: None named; no application was pending as of adoption.
outcome: Buffalo Township Board of Supervisors created a municipal curative amendment, giving the township 180 days to draft data-center zoning rules and effectively barring new data-center proposals during that period.

date_enacted: Board of Supervisors adopted Resolution No. 05122026 on 2026-05-12.
duration: Declares the township zoning ordinance substantively invalid for not defining or regulating data centers, triggering a 180-day municipal curative-amendment period during which new data center applications are paused from vesting under the prior ordinance.
legal_basis: Resolution No. 05122026, Municipal Curative Amendment (Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code Section 609.2)
trigger: Zoning ordinance did not define or regulate data centers.
current_status: Active as of 2026-07-31; 180-day curative-amendment period from 2026-05-12.

date_enacted: Board of Supervisors voted unanimously at its regular meeting on Wednesday, 2026-06-10, to approve a curative amendment. Confirmed directly by the Butler Eagle's meeting report, which quotes Supervisors Phil Wulff, Don Pringle, and Mark Lauer on the record from that meeting.
duration: 180-day pause halting data center and power-generation-plant-system development while the township prepares zoning standards.
legal_basis: Curative amendment approved by the Board of Supervisors on 2026-06-10, halting data center and power-generation-plant-system development for 180 days (Supervisor Phil Wulff: 'the board of supervisors needs to undertake formal action to remedy an exclusionary omission... in the zoning ordinance'). A July 31, 2026 Butler Eagle roundup of Butler County municipalities independently confirms Center Township (along with Adams Township) 'went as far as enacting 180-day moratoriums on data centers and related developments.' Specific resolution/ordinance number and official minutes were not located in sources reviewed.
trigger: No data center development request had been received; adopted proactively.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its computed 180-day expiry (~2026-12-07). No data center application had been filed in Center Township as of adoption; the pause was adopted proactively, alongside similar action in neighboring Adams Township, while Center, Summit, Jefferson, Penn, Lancaster, and Forward townships in Butler County all worked on data-center zoning ordinances as of the July 31, 2026 countywide roundup. No news of a permanent ordinance adoption, extension, or repeal specific to Center Township was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.

date_enacted: 2026-04-30, Clinton Township Board of Supervisors vote to put a six-month moratorium in place while reviewing a draft data-center ordinance (Wayne County); exact duration in calendar days not confirmed in sources reviewed.
duration: Approximately six months (treated here as 180 days) from the April 30, 2026 vote, to allow the township and Wayne County Planning Commissions to review a draft data-center/SALDO ordinance before adoption.
legal_basis: Clinton Township Board of Supervisors vote (April 30, 2026 meeting) adopting a six-month moratorium on data-center applications while a draft Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance (SALDO) amendment, prepared by Solicitor Jeffrey Treat since a December 2025 request, is reviewed by the Township and Wayne County Planning Commissions (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed).
trigger: Specific project combined with a regulatory gap: the moratorium was adopted the same day Linde Corporation submitted a proposal for a data center and gas-fired power plants on a 758-acre former mining parcel near Browndale, on land identified as containing one of only two 'exceptional value waters' streams in Wayne County (Roger's Creek, tributary to the Lackawanna/Susquehanna); the township had already been drafting data-center standards since a December 2025 board request.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; the moratorium's precise end date is not independently confirmed (estimated late October 2026 from a six-month term starting April 30, 2026). Since adoption, Linde Corporation's application (submitted the same day as the moratorium) proceeded through contested public hearings, including a May 7, 2026 planning commission session drawing roughly 250 attendees. On 2026-09-14, the Board of Supervisors -- following a unanimous Planning Commission recommendation to deny -- unanimously rejected Linde's preliminary land development plan for 20 data center buildings and two gas-fired power plants, finding it did not meet the township's Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance (insufficient detail on environmental protections, stormwater management, and infrastructure impacts). Linde is widely expected to appeal to Wayne County Court. [VERIFY instrument number; primary source (news-only evidence) not confirmed at confidence 0.65 in the 2026-09 refresh]
affected_projects: Linde Corporation's proposed $6 billion data center and two gas-fired power plants on 758 acres of former mining land near Browndale; the application was submitted April 30, 2026 (the same day the moratorium was adopted) and was unanimously rejected by the Board of Supervisors on 2026-09-14 for failing to meet SALDO standards; an appeal to Wayne County Court is expected.
outcome: Clinton Township (Wayne County) Board of Supervisors voted on 2026-04-30 to impose a six-month moratorium on data-center applications while it finalized a data-center ordinance; the township separately and unanimously rejected the pending Linde Corporation data center/power-plant land development plan on 2026-09-14 for failing to meet subdivision and land development standards.

date_enacted: 2026-07-07, Conewago Township Board of Supervisors, unanimous vote adopting Resolution 2026-13 (York County)
duration: 180-day moratorium on all data center applications, per the township's own presentation materials.
legal_basis: Resolution 2026-13 (Conewago Township, York County), adopted unanimously at the July 7, 2026 Board of Supervisors meeting, invoking the municipal curative-amendment process to prevent a developer from filing a substantive validity challenge to the township's zoning ordinance over its silence on data centers.
trigger: Regulatory gap: zoning ordinance did not address data centers; a draft data-center ordinance and zoning overlay map, developed with township counsel (Eckert Seamans) and engineering consultant (CS Davidson), was presented to the public at a July 23, 2026 special joint meeting of the Board of Supervisors and Planning Commission.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its official 2027-01-03 end date (per the township's own presentation). A draft ordinance establishing a Data Center Overlay district (100-acre minimum parcel, 250-foot perimeter setback, 90-foot height cap, 50-foot landscaped buffer, acoustic standards, etc.) has been presented publicly but not yet adopted as of this research pass; residents continue to organize opposition to rezoning for data centers in the township.
affected_projects: None named; a prior 2025 proposal to rezone land near Bible Baptist Church for a data center (developer identified in some coverage) drew opposition but is treated separately from this proactive, township-wide moratorium.
outcome: Conewago Township Board of Supervisors unanimously adopted Resolution 2026-13 on 2026-07-07, a 180-day moratorium on data-center applications (ending 2027-01-03), while it develops a Data Center Overlay zoning ordinance.

date_enacted: 2025-08-11, Dorrance Township Board of Supervisors, unanimous vote (Luzerne County)
duration: Up to 180 days from Aug. 11, 2025 to amend the zoning ordinance; the process concluded early when the township adopted a permanent zoning amendment on 2025-09-22 (about six weeks later).
legal_basis: Dorrance Township Board of Supervisors ordinance (adopted 2025-08-11) imposing 'a temporary moratorium of the acceptance, processing, and approval of applications for data centers and similar technology, related businesses that consume large amounts of power and use water for cooling, throughout all zoning districts of the township'; superseded by a permanent zoning amendment adopted 2025-09-22 (unanimous 3-0 vote) establishing conditional-use standards for data centers, data center accessory structures, power substations, and data center campuses.
trigger: Regulatory gap combined with public pressure: zoning ordinance was silent on data centers; adopted after more than 100 residents packed a planning commission meeting following rumors that a data center was planned for the township, though officials said no proposal had been received.
current_status: Replaced as of 2025-09-22. The township's Aug. 11, 2025 temporary moratorium was superseded about six weeks later when supervisors voted 3-0 to permanently amend the zoning ordinance's conditional-use standards to regulate data centers, data center accessory structures, power substations, and data center campuses (covering noise, vibration, traffic and police/fire impact, and a water feasibility study requirement). The permanent amendment was later challenged by developer Brewster Land Company (landowner curative amendment / validity challenge over a 155-acre B-2-zoned parcel); the Zoning Hearing Board rejected that challenge (outcome reported as a township 'win' around 2026-05/06), and the developer has since appealed to court (as of an Aug. 31, 2026 report).
affected_projects: None named as pending at the original moratorium's adoption. The subsequent zoning-validity challenge came from Brewster Land Company over a 155-acre B-2 parcel, adjudicated separately by the Zoning Hearing Board and later appealed to court by the developer.
outcome: Dorrance Township Board of Supervisors adopted a temporary moratorium on data-center applications on 2025-08-11, which was replaced about six weeks later by a permanent zoning amendment (2025-09-22) establishing conditional-use standards for data centers, data center accessory structures, power substations, and data center campuses.

date_enacted: 2026-06-16, Doylestown Township Board of Supervisors vote (Bucks County)
duration: 180 days (six months) from June 16, 2026 to adopt new data-center zoning rules; during that time no data-center application may be submitted or reviewed in the township.
legal_basis: Doylestown Township Board of Supervisors resolution (adopted June 16, 2026) invoking the municipal curative amendment process, declaring the zoning ordinance's failure to identify or regulate data centers 'substantively invalid' (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed); township solicitor Peter Nelson advised the process requires adoption of a new ordinance within 180 days and bars reuse of the same curative-amendment tool for three years.
trigger: Regulatory gap: zoning ordinance does not identify or regulate data centers as a permitted use; adopted proactively as part of a broader wave of Bucks County municipalities (following neighboring Falls Township's contested Amazon data center) acting to define and regulate the use before an application arrives.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23, nearing its computed 2026-12-13 end date. The vote does not itself adopt final zoning rules; it starts a 180-day period for officials and consultants to draft standards on where data centers may be located, how they are defined, and what development standards would apply. No application is pending in the township.
affected_projects: None; no data center application is pending in Doylestown Township.
outcome: Doylestown Township Board of Supervisors voted on June 16, 2026 to begin a 180-day municipal curative amendment process, temporarily freezing any data-center applications while the township drafts zoning rules.

date_enacted: 2026-03, East Whiteland Township Board of Supervisors vote to initiate a municipal curative amendment (Chester County); exact day not confirmed in sources reviewed
duration: 180 days from the March 2026 vote to draft and adopt a data-center zoning ordinance ('Data Center Ordinance'); a public hearing to consider its adoption was set for Sept. 24, 2026.
legal_basis: East Whiteland Township municipal curative amendment under the PA Municipalities Planning Code, developed with a resident working group beginning May 2026; a Sept. 24, 2026 public hearing was set to consider adoption of the resulting ordinance
trigger: Regulatory gap combined with a specific, highly contested project: developer Green Fig's proposal (later expanded to 1.7 million sq ft) for a data center on Swedesford Road, which drew sustained community opposition; the township already had an earlier, separately approved 2024 data-center plan on the same site.
current_status: Nearing resolution as of 2026-09-23. The 180-day curative-amendment clock started in March 2026 (per The Center Square); Green Fig withdrew its expanded 1.7-million-sq-ft application in May 2026 amid sustained opposition and signaled intent to instead pursue its earlier, previously approved 2024 plan. A resident working group helped draft the resulting 'Data Center Ordinance,' for which the Board of Supervisors set a Sept. 24, 2026 public hearing to consider adoption (one day after this research pass); the pending Sentinel/Green Fig application is not on that hearing's agenda.
affected_projects: Green Fig/Sentinel data center proposal on Swedesford Road; the expanded 1.7-million-sq-ft version was withdrawn in May 2026, with the developer expected to instead pursue its earlier-approved 2024 plan (details of that plan not confirmed in this pass).
outcome: East Whiteland Township Board of Supervisors initiated a municipal curative amendment in March 2026 to add data-center zoning standards; a resident working group helped draft the resulting ordinance, which was scheduled for a Sept. 24, 2026 adoption hearing.

date_enacted: 2026-07-27, Falls Township Board of Supervisors vote (Bucks County)
duration: 180 days from July 27, 2026 for the township to review and potentially amend Chapter 209 of its zoning ordinance regarding data centers.
legal_basis: Falls Township Board of Supervisors resolution (adopted July 27, 2026) declaring a portion of the zoning ordinance 'substantively invalid' as to data centers, initiating a municipal curative amendment as a 'protective measure' against substantive-validity challenges (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed).
trigger: Regulatory gap combined with sustained public opposition to the already-approved Amazon Web Services data center (a 2-million-square-foot, 10-building campus under construction at the former U.S. Steel/Keystone Trade Center site); residents demanded clearer definitions of 'data center' and infrastructure/utility standards for future proposals.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its computed 2027-01-23 end date. The curative amendment does not affect the already-approved (March 2025) Amazon Web Services data center, which remains under construction; township staff will review the existing zoning ordinance and bring proposed amendments back to the Board within 180 days, with drafts to be posted publicly and advertised before hearings.
affected_projects: None going forward; the curative amendment explicitly does not affect the already-approved and under-construction Amazon Web Services data center at the former U.S. Steel site, whose approval (March 2025) and community pushback prompted this action.
outcome: Falls Township Board of Supervisors voted July 27, 2026 to declare part of its zoning ordinance substantively invalid as to data centers, opening a 180-day curative-amendment period to draft new zoning rules.

date_enacted: 2026-08-20, Gregg Township Board of Supervisors, special meeting, unanimous adoption of Resolution 2026-03
duration: Not to exceed 180 days, or until earlier terminated by the Board of Supervisors; bars new data center or 'technical development' applications while a curative amendment to the zoning ordinance is completed. Excludes the pending PNK Group application, which continues to be processed separately.
legal_basis: Resolution 2026-03 (Gregg Township, Union County), adopted at an Aug. 20, 2026 special meeting
trigger: Curative-amendment process to add data-center zoning standards, prompted by PNK Group's pending application for a large data-center campus at Great Stream Commons and the absence of applicable standards in the township's zoning ordinance.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Adopted unanimously at an Aug. 20, 2026 special meeting; bars new data center/technical development applications for up to 180 days (through approximately 2027-02-16) while the township completes a curative amendment. Does not apply to PNK Group's pending application, which continues to be processed and has been the subject of contested public hearings (through at least Aug. 25, 2026), including reports that several formerly opposed neighboring households signed non-opposition or support letters after a confidential settlement offer from PNK.
affected_projects: PNK Group's pending application for a data center at Great Stream Commons (an initial 60-megawatt phase with a full build-out up to 240 megawatts) is expressly excluded from the moratorium and continues to be processed.
outcome: Gregg Township (Union County) Board of Supervisors adopted Resolution 2026-03, a moratorium on new data-center applications (excluding the pending PNK Group application), to allow time to complete a curative amendment to the zoning ordinance.

date_enacted: 2026-06-08, Hazle Township (Luzerne County) Board of Supervisors, unanimous vote adopting a curative amendment.
duration: 180 days from adoption (to approximately 2026-12-05).
legal_basis: Municipal curative amendment adopted by the Hazle Township Board of Supervisors, temporarily invalidating portions of the township zoning ordinance for 180 days on the stated grounds that the ordinance is deficient because it does not address data centers (instrument number not located).
trigger: Followed sustained community opposition ("Project Hazelnot") to NorthPoint Development's proposed ~1,300-acre, 15-building "Project Hazelnut" data-center campus with substation, which the township had already rejected in November 2025 and which a Luzerne County judge ruled against in spring 2026.
current_status: Active as of 2026-07-31 (expires approximately 2026-12-05).
affected_projects: NorthPoint Development's proposed 'Project Hazelnut' data-center campus, previously denied by the township and by a county court.
outcome: Board of Supervisors unanimously adopted a 180-day curative amendment pausing consideration of new data-center applications while permanent zoning language is drafted.

date_enacted: 2026-07-14, Little Britain Township Board of Supervisors, unanimous vote adopting the formal moratorium resolution (Lancaster County); preceded by a June 9, 2026 preliminary vote to move forward with the same moratorium concept.
duration: 180 days from the July 14, 2026 resolution, preventing submission of any applications for data centers, their ancillary structures, or energy generation, while the township develops a zoning ordinance.
legal_basis: Little Britain Township Board of Supervisors resolution (adopted July 14, 2026) declaring existing ordinances invalid regarding data centers and related uses because they are not addressed, initiating a municipal curative amendment (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed).
trigger: Regulatory gap: the township has no ordinance specifically addressing data centers; adopted proactively while the board develops a new ordinance modeled on those of nearby townships.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its computed 2027-01-10 end date. The township now has six months from adoption to develop an ordinance amendment with help from the township solicitor and planning commission, using nearby townships' ordinances as models. No news of an extension, adoption of the amendment, or repeal was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
affected_projects: None named; adopted proactively rather than in response to a pending application.
outcome: Little Britain Township Board of Supervisors unanimously adopted a resolution on 2026-07-14 imposing a 180-day moratorium on data-center applications, following a preliminary June 9, 2026 vote to move forward with the concept.

date_enacted: County commissioners reportedly approved a curative-amendment resolution on 2026-06-18.
duration: 180-day municipal curative-amendment period after declaring the county zoning ordinance substantially invalid for lacking appropriate regulation of data centers and related uses; affects municipalities participating in the county zoning partnership.
legal_basis: Resolution 2026-16 (Lycoming County), adopted 3-0 by the Board of Commissioners at its regular public meeting on 2026-06-18, declaring the county's zoning ordinance (enacted 1991, amended 2021) 'substantially invalid' for failing to provide appropriate zoning regulation of data centers and accessory/similar uses, and triggering the 180-day curative-amendment period under the PA Municipalities Planning Code.
trigger: County zoning ordinance lacked appropriate regulation of data centers and related uses.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its 180-day statutory ceiling (~2026-12-15). The county's Planning & Community Development Department, working with consultant Entech Engineering, introduced a full draft curative amendment (covering power sourcing, water supply, permitted zones, setbacks, noise, and decommissioning) to the County Planning Commission in September 2026; Commission Chair Jason Bogle stressed it remains a draft, and public-comment hearings before the Board of Commissioners were expected to begin around mid-November 2026, ahead of the statutory deadline. Commissioner Marc Sortman has repeatedly clarified that the county's own zoning authority covers only the 19 municipalities in its zoning partnership (which does not include Muncy Township, a separate PA MPC curative-amendment moratorium already tracked in this inventory as pa-muncy-township-2026); other municipalities must adopt their own ordinances.

duration: 180 days, expiring about 2026-05-17 unless extended or superseded
legal_basis: Resolution R-11-19-2025 (the moratorium, now superseded); Ordinance No. 1-2026, the 'Data Center Land Use Ordinance,' enacted by the Montour County Board of Commissioners on April 14, 2026, amending the County Zoning Ordinance to define and regulate Data Centers and Data Center Accessory Uses.
trigger: Concern over potential data centers or similar large-scale digital/technology facilities; county needed time for Planning Commission ad-hoc committee ordinance work
current_status: Superseded. The Montour County Board of Commissioners enacted Ordinance No. 1-2026 ('Data Center Land Use Ordinance') on April 14, 2026 -- before the moratorium's own nominal 2026-05-17 expiration -- amending the County Zoning Ordinance to permit Data Centers as a Conditional Use in the Industrial Zoning District, subject to detailed siting, setback/buffer-yard, noise, lighting, and 'Sensitive Receptor' protections and a Conditional Use review process. The moratorium (Resolution R-11-19-2025) is no longer the operative instrument; Ordinance 1-2026 governs data center siting in Montour County as of 2026-07-31.
affected_projects: No pending data center applications at enactment; Talen Energy later sought rezoning of Anthony Township parcels for a data-center-related industrial use
outcome: Following the 2026-02-12 denial of Talen Energy's zoning map amendment, the county completed and enacted the Data Center Land Use Ordinance (Ordinance 1-2026) on 2026-04-14, permitting data centers by conditional use in the Industrial Zoning District rather than prohibiting them outright.

date_enacted: 2026-07-21, Morrisville Borough Council, vote to adopt the curative amendment (Bucks County)
duration: 180-day waiting period from July 21, 2026 to review land-use impacts and adopt updated data-center zoning regulations.
legal_basis: Morrisville Borough Council resolution (adopted July 21, 2026) declaring a portion of the borough's zoning ordinance invalid and initiating a municipal curative amendment under the PA Municipalities Planning Code to shield the borough from data-center-related zoning challenges (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed).
trigger: Regulatory gap, adopted in the same week as neighboring Falls Township's similar action amid broader Bucks County concern over data-center energy consumption, noise, and water usage.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its computed 2027-01-17 end date. The borough plans to use the 180-day period to review land-use impacts and prepare new zoning regulations related to data-center development; no application is reported pending in the borough.
affected_projects: None named; adopted proactively.
outcome: Morrisville Borough Council adopted a resolution on 2026-07-21 declaring part of its zoning ordinance invalid and opening a 180-day curative-amendment/waiting period to draft data-center zoning regulations.

date_enacted: 2026-05-18, Mount Carmel Township Board of Supervisors, unanimous vote (Northumberland County)
duration: 180 days from May 18, 2026 to complete a municipal curative amendment ('Zoning Amendment') addressing data centers.
legal_basis: Mount Carmel Township municipal curative amendment under the PA Municipalities Planning Code; the township's own site describes it simply as the '180 day moratorium enacted on May 18, 2026,' the end result of which will be a curative amendment to correct zoning invalidities regarding data centers (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed).
trigger: Regulatory gap combined with sustained community opposition: hundreds of residents packed public meetings (including a May 13, 2026 hearing) opposing data-center development in the township; officials say they cannot outright ban the use but are working to limit and define it through zoning.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23, nearing its computed 2026-11-14 end date. The township presented an ordinance work-progress update on July 15, 2026 and a preliminary draft ordinance update on Aug. 12, 2026; a public hearing for comment only (no board vote that night) was advertised for Sept. 23, 2026 at Mount Carmel Area High School. No news of an extension, adoption of the final ordinance, or repeal was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
affected_projects: None named as pending at adoption; the moratorium responded to general community opposition and rumors of data-center interest in the township rather than a specific filed application.
outcome: Mount Carmel Township Board of Supervisors adopted a 180-day moratorium on data-center proposals on 2026-05-18 to allow time to draft a curative-amendment zoning ordinance, with a public-comment hearing on the draft ordinance held Sept. 23, 2026.

date_enacted: Board of Supervisors approved a temporary moratorium at an April 28, 2026 special meeting; reported by the Sun-Gazette on 2026-05-01.
duration: Nine months, or until the township adopts zoning regulations addressing data centers, whichever occurs first. Bars acceptance or review of listed municipal applications for data centers, data center campuses, high-intensity data processing facilities, and substantially similar uses during that period.
legal_basis: Board of Supervisors motion/temporary moratorium adopted at the April 28, 2026 special meeting; no separately numbered ordinance or resolution identified in the sources reviewed
trigger: Lack of existing zoning provisions addressing data centers.
current_status: Active as of 2026-07-31; nine-month pause from the 2026-04-28 vote runs to approximately late January 2027 unless superseded by earlier zoning adoption.

date_enacted: 2026-05-06, Smithfield Township Board of Supervisors, adoption of Resolution No. 621 (Monroe County)
duration: Up to 180 days from May 6, 2026 (statutory ceiling Nov. 2, 2026) to adopt curative zoning amendments for data centers, data center accessory uses, and disaster recovery facilities; the process concluded early when the Board adopted the resulting curative amendment on 2026-08-12.
legal_basis: Resolution No. 621 (Smithfield Township), formally initiating the Municipalities Planning Code curative-amendment process; superseded by the curative amendment adopted 2026-08-12 establishing a new H-1 (Heavy Industrial) Zoning District for data centers, data center accessory uses, and disaster recovery facilities
trigger: Regulatory gap: zoning ordinance did not specifically address data centers; adopted proactively to develop tailored standards and a dedicated zoning district.
current_status: Replaced as of 2026-08-12. Resolution No. 621 (adopted 2026-05-06) opened a 180-day curative-amendment window (statutory ceiling 2026-11-02); following an Aug. 12, 2026 public hearing, the Board of Supervisors adopted the resulting curative amendment early, creating a new H-1 (Heavy Industrial) Zoning District (carved from the southern portion of the existing M-1 Industrial District) as the only zone where data centers, data center accessory uses, and disaster recovery facilities may locate (as Conditional Uses); these uses are no longer permitted in the township's ED or M-1 districts. The Board said it will address additional concerns in a future amendment.
affected_projects: None named; adopted proactively.
outcome: Smithfield Township Board of Supervisors adopted Resolution No. 621, opening a municipal curative-amendment window that it used to adopt (on 2026-08-12, ahead of the Nov. 2, 2026 deadline) a permanent zoning amendment confining data centers to a newly created H-1 Heavy Industrial District.

date_enacted: 2026-05, Upper Burrell Township Board of Supervisors (Westmoreland County); exact day not confirmed in sources reviewed
duration: 180 days; does not apply to building permits already granted to TECfusions for work on its existing 'Building J' (already operational), and did not prevent the township from later approving a land development plan (Aug. 5, 2026) for further electrical/mechanical upgrades to that building. Ends 2026-11-02.
legal_basis: Upper Burrell Township municipal curative amendment/moratorium on new data-center development (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed)
trigger: Public pressure over TECfusions' 'Keystone Connect' hyperscale data-center campus (up to 1,400 acres, potentially up to 3 gigawatts, at the former Alcoa/Arconic Technical Center); residents sought more transparency and regulation before further development.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23, ending 2026-11-02. Bars new data-center development but does not apply to TECfusions' existing Building J permits (already operational, delivering GPU capacity per an Aug. 27, 2026 company release) or to a land-development plan the township approved Aug. 5, 2026 for further work on that building. A new draft ordinance (H-1-style Heavy Industrial standards, noise/vibration studies, and a contested requirement that developers provide their own baseload power generation) was under Planning Commission review, with a meeting held Sept. 15, 2026. A land-use appeal (Protect PT and two New Kensington residents, filed in Westmoreland County Court of Common Pleas) argues the township improperly allowed TECfusions' expansion to proceed via permits and a land-development-plan approval without requiring a full zoning/special-exception process.
affected_projects: TECfusions' 'Keystone Connect' campus at the former Alcoa/Arconic Technical Center (up to 1,400 acres, potentially up to 3 GW); Building J is already operational and exempted from the moratorium, and a land-development plan for further work on that building was approved Aug. 5, 2026 despite the moratorium.
outcome: Upper Burrell Township Board of Supervisors adopted a 180-day moratorium/curative amendment on new data-center development (excluding already-permitted TECfusions work), to allow time to draft a data-center zoning ordinance; a land-use appeal challenging the township's handling of TECfusions' existing permits is pending in Westmoreland County court.

date_enacted: Board of Supervisors adopted Resolution 2026-09 on 2026-05-13, formally ratifying an administrative pause the township says began with a March 11, 2026 motion.
duration: Pause on applications for data center-related uses while the township prepares tailored zoning standards and pursues a municipal curative amendment. No explicit day count for the pause was located.
legal_basis: Resolution 2026-09 (adopted 2026-05-13), formally ratifying the March 11, 2026 administrative pause on Data Center Uses under PA Municipalities Planning Code (MPC) Section 609.2, followed by Resolution 2026-15, which sets forth the specific findings of substantive invalidity required within 30 days under Section 609.2. Resolution 2026-15's own text states it was 'DULY PRESENTED AND ADOPTED...at a public meeting on the 10 day of June, 2026,' but the Township's own June 12, 2026 public notice and its July 8, 2026 Board of Supervisors agenda both list 'Resolution 2026-15-609.2 of the MPC-Administrative pause' as an item scheduled for a motion/vote at the July 8, 2026 meeting; the exact adoption date is therefore uncertain (between 2026-06-10 and 2026-07-08), a discrepancy in the Township's own records that could not be resolved from documents reviewed in this pass.
trigger: Township preparing tailored zoning standards for data centers.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. The administrative pause on Data Center Uses (begun by a March 11, 2026 motion, ratified by Resolution 2026-09 on May 13, 2026) remains in force; the Township adopted Resolution 2026-15 (setting out the statutorily required specific findings of invalidity under MPC Section 609.2) around June-July 2026, renewing the Planning Commission's, Zoning Officer's, Township Manager's, Solicitor's, and Engineer's authorization to prepare a curative amendment to the Zoning Ordinance. No fixed end date is stated; the pause runs until a curative amendment is adopted. A third-party tracker (savrn.com, Pennsylvania Data Center Moratorium Tracker) independently lists Warrington Township's status as unchanged -- 'Local moratorium on data centers until a condition is met' -- as of its most recent update, citing this same Resolution 2026-15. A separate secondary aggregator (Civic IQ) surfaced a claim that the Township adopted 'Resolution 2026-19' on Aug. 11, 2026 extending the moratorium 180 days; that claim could not be corroborated and, on inspection, the underlying Civic IQ page is misattributed to a 'Town of York charter' in Michigan rather than Warrington Township, York County, Pennsylvania, so it is disregarded as unreliable.

date_enacted: 2026-09-15, West Mahanoy Township Board of Supervisors, unanimous vote (Schuylkill County)
duration: 180 days. Per the adopted resolution's text, the township 'shall not be required to entertain or consider any landowner's curative amendment or proposals for a data center use or solar farm' during that period.
legal_basis: West Mahanoy Township Board of Supervisors resolution invoking the municipal curative amendment process under the PA Municipalities Planning Code, declaring the zoning ordinance invalid as it relates to data centers, solar farms, on-site power generation, and related accessory uses (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed)
trigger: Regulatory gap: the zoning ordinance does not explicitly permit or provide standards for data centers or solar farms ('we don't have the protections in place'); adopted proactively, with no application pending, amid data-center and warehouse-development activity in neighboring Butler and Kline townships.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Adopted unanimously on 2026-09-15, covering both data centers and solar farms (plus on-site power generation and accessory uses); the township hired Siana Law as special zoning counsel, with a draft corrective ordinance (addressing noise, buffers, power sources, and community benefits) expected the following month. No application for either use is currently pending.
affected_projects: None; officials confirmed no application for a data center or solar farm was pending as of adoption. Nearby, data-center-related developments are proceeding under warehouse permits in Butler and Kline townships.
outcome: West Mahanoy Township Board of Supervisors adopted a resolution declaring its zoning ordinance invalid as to data centers and solar farms, triggering a 180-day municipal curative-amendment period during which no applications for either use will be entertained.

date_enacted: 2026-05, West Whiteland Township Board of Supervisors vote to invoke a municipal curative amendment (Chester County); exact day not confirmed, reported to the Planning Commission as already invoked on 2026-05-05
duration: 180 days from adoption to adopt corrective zoning amendments addressing data centers.
legal_basis: West Whiteland Township municipal curative amendment under the PA Municipalities Planning Code, declaring the zoning ordinance deficient for regulating data centers (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed)
trigger: Regulatory gap: zoning ordinance did not address data centers; adopted proactively, with no application pending, following neighboring East Whiteland Township's contested Green Fig data-center dispute.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23, nearing its 2026-11-01 end date. Township planning staff told the Planning Commission on May 5, 2026 that the Board of Supervisors had invoked the municipal cure; the draft ordinance under development uses a 20,000-sq-ft threshold (excluding small server rooms), a dbC low-frequency noise standard, and was informed by model language PennFuture prepared for Allegheny County. No application is pending. [VERIFY instrument number; primary source (news-only evidence) not confirmed at confidence 0.68 in the 2026-09 refresh]
affected_projects: None; no data center application is pending in West Whiteland.
outcome: West Whiteland Township Board of Supervisors invoked a municipal curative amendment declaring its zoning ordinance deficient for regulating data centers, giving the township 180 days (through approximately Nov. 1, 2026) to adopt corrective standards.

date_enacted: 2026-07-09, Williamsport City Council, 6-0 vote adopting Resolution #10088 (Lycoming County)
duration: 180 days from adoption to enact a curative amendment under 53 P.S. Section 10609.2, with a follow-up resolution required within 30 days making specific findings of invalidity. Councilman Milliken characterized it as effectively 'hitting pause' on data-center development even though the resolution does not describe itself as a 'pause.'
legal_basis: Resolution #10088 (City of Williamsport), adopted 6-0 by City Council on July 9, 2026, declaring the city's Zoning Ordinance (enacted April 16, 1998, amended since) substantively invalid insofar as it excludes data centers and ancillary buildings or uses, including but not limited to power generating facilities, and proposing preparation of a curative amendment under 53 P.S. Section 10609.2; a follow-up Resolution #10091 was required within 30 days to make specific findings of the declared invalidity.
trigger: Regulatory gap: 1998 zoning ordinance does not account for data centers or their accessory uses; adopted proactively, following similar curative-amendment action by Lycoming County and several county townships, to close the loophole that would otherwise let a developer file a landowner curative amendment and force approval of a data center anywhere in the city.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its computed 2027-01-05 end date. No data center is presently planned in the City of Williamsport; the resolution was the city's opening move in a regional contest over who regulates data-center siting, alongside Lycoming County's own curative amendment (pa-lycoming-county-2026, a separate, already-tracked instrument covering the county's 19 zoning-partner municipalities, which does not include the City of Williamsport).
affected_projects: None; no data center application is pending in the City of Williamsport as of adoption.
outcome: Williamsport City Council adopted Resolution #10088 on 2026-07-09, a 6-0 vote declaring the city's zoning ordinance substantively invalid as to data centers and opening a 180-day curative-amendment period.

date_enacted: 2026-07-27 (Town Council public hearing and approval by voice vote at its regular meeting)
duration: One year upon passage, or as otherwise provided by the Town Council by ordinance; effective immediately upon passage
legal_basis: Town of Westerly ordinance 'AN ORDINANCE IMPOSING A ONE-YEAR MORATORIUM ON ALL DATA CENTERS,' adding a new Data Center Moratorium section to the Westerly Code of Ordinances; noticed for public hearing 2026-07-27, adopted the same night by voice vote
trigger: Town's ordinances and zoning regulations are silent on data centers; officials anticipate data center applications given the town's undeveloped land near water bodies and wanted time to draft siting/zoning rules before any application could vest
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. The Westerly Town Council adopted a one-year moratorium on all data centers by voice vote at its July 27, 2026 meeting after a public hearing at which no one spoke in opposition. The ordinance bars the Planning Board, Zoning Board of Review, Zoning Board of Appeal, and all town agencies/employees from accepting, processing, approving, denying, or otherwise acting on any non-vested application, plan, permit, or license for a data center for one year from passage (through approximately 2027-07-27), with a vesting exemption for applications already certified complete.
affected_projects: None named; the town manager told the council the ordinances are 'currently silent on data centers' and the pause is meant to give the zoning side time to draft rules before any application could vest.
outcome: Adopted by voice vote after a public hearing at the July 27, 2026 regular Town Council meeting; no recorded opposition.

date_enacted: August 18, 2026 (County Council third reading, per county's own Aug. 18, 2026 agenda packet and Fox Carolina/WYFF4/WSPA coverage of the unanimous-report vote; first reading was a special called meeting June 29, 2026)
duration: Six months
legal_basis: Ordinance No. 2026-037 (Anderson County Council)
trigger: County has no regulatory framework or zoning structure for data centers; concern over strain on the electric power grid, water supply, and local infrastructure from inadequately regulated development of multiple data centers.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; adopted on third reading Aug. 18, 2026 and confirmed via the county's own agenda packet and multiple news organizations. No pending items or new applications for data centers may be accepted, processed, or approved for the moratorium's term.
outcome: Adopted six-month moratorium on acceptance, processing, or approval of data center development applications.

date_enacted: July 20, 2026 (County Council unanimous approval, per WSOC-TV, following a June 15, 2026 first reading)
duration: Six months
legal_basis: Ordinance 2026-14 (Chester County Council), "Declaring a temporary, countywide pause on the acceptance, processing, and approval of applications regarding data centers and data center-related developments; directing the study and preparation of data center development standards; invoking the pending ordinance doctrine"; first reading and public hearing June 15/July 20, 2026 per the county's own July 20, 2026 council agenda packet, third reading approved July 20, 2026.
trigger: Pause to allow the county to develop rules and guidelines, with public educational meetings planned to begin in August 2026; first-reading materials cited electric-grid and utility capacity, economic, environmental, and community effects.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; confirmed via the county's own July 20, 2026 council agenda packet (Ordinance 2026-14, public hearing and 3rd reading that date) and WBTV news coverage of the unanimous vote. The 180-day term (from July 20, 2026) runs to approximately 2027-01-16 and had not lapsed as of 2026-09-23; no extension, repeal, or replacement was found. The county's June 18, 2026 press release also notes the pause followed the county's separately adopted data-center zoning regulations (CCTA26-06).
outcome: Approved six-month moratorium on new data center development.

date_enacted: June 1, 2026 (County Council third reading and public hearing, adopting Ordinance 25-26-23)
duration: Until January 1, 2028, or until the county adopts regulations for data center/data processing/cryptocurrency mining uses, whichever occurs first
legal_basis: Ordinance 25-26-23 (Chesterfield County Council)
trigger: Immediately stops acceptance, review, or action on zoning approvals, construction permits, site plans, and other county approvals for data centers, data processing facilities, cryptocurrency mining operations, and related uses in unincorporated Chesterfield County; followed an emergency moratorium adopted April 6, 2026.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; regular ordinance (No. 25-26-23) replacing an April 6, 2026 emergency moratorium, in effect until 2028-01-01 or earlier adoption of permanent regulations. Confirmed against the county's own ordinance text ("shall remain in effect until January 1, 2028, or until such time as the County adopts regulations governing these uses, whichever occurs first") and the county's current ordinances index, which lists no later ordinance amending or repealing 25-26-23 through its most recent entry (09/14/2026).
outcome: Adopted long-term temporary moratorium on data center and related approvals in unincorporated Chesterfield County.

date_enacted: September 14, 2026 (County Council third and final reading and public hearing, per WIS; second reading was at an Aug. 24, 2026 special called meeting, first reading Aug. 10, 2026)
duration: Six months
legal_basis: Ordinance 2026-18 (Clarendon County Council)
trigger: County's Unified Development Code does not specifically define data centers or battery energy storage systems; council sought to close a loophole after learning of a proposed "Project 59" data center in the county industrial park, and to give time to set standards for setbacks, buffers, noise, lighting, and emergency access.

Before the original 120-day term lapsed, the City Commission gave first reading to a 60-day extension ordinance (reported by KRGV on 2026-08-25 as approved 'last week') and a second/final reading roughly two weeks later, extending the moratorium to the 180-day statutory maximum (through approximately December 2026) while a contracted engineering firm (Ambiotec Engineering) completes a water/wastewater/electrical infrastructure impact study. The moratorium has no effect on the Fluidstack- and Eneus Energy-linked data center projects proposed just outside city limits near the Port of Harlingen/Valley International Airport, since those sites are in unincorporated Cameron County, outside the city's zoning jurisdiction (per Mayor Norma Sepulveda, 2026-09). No numbered city ordinance ('Ordinance No. ___') for either the original moratorium or the extension was located on harlingentx.gov or in news coverage reviewed, so the instrument-number portion of the original VERIFY marker remains open.
affected_projects: None formally proposed within Harlingen city limits as of the moratorium's adoption, per Rio Grande Guardian reporting
outcome: 120-day moratorium adopted to study potential data center impacts and modernize land use regulations

date_enacted: 2026-05-12 (Hill County Commissioners Court approved a 1-year moratorium on data center construction, per KWTX)
duration: One year (as adopted; rescinded before completing its term)
legal_basis: Commissioners Court order
trigger: Development pressure from multiple (reportedly up to eight) proposed data center projects in a rural North Texas county
current_status: Rescinded. Following a $100 million federal lawsuit filed by a data center developer (~2026-05-28) alleging the moratorium was illegal, the Hill County Commissioners Court voted to rescind the moratorium on 2026-06-04 and adopted new data center review requirements/policies instead (per KWTX, KCENTV, KXXV, and The Texas Tribune). affected_projects: Multiple proposed data center projects in Hill County; the specific developer plaintiff in the $100 million lawsuit is described in coverage as 'RCM Hill'
outcome: One-year moratorium adopted 2026-05-12; rescinded 2026-06-04 under litigation pressure and replaced with new development-review policies

trigger: regulatory_gap and specific_project concerns, driven by a citizen petition ('Save Lubbock' group led by Stephen Sanders); Council members cited ERCOT grid conditions and a desire to await further state-level guidance/regulation before large-scale data center development proceeds.
current_status: Pending as of 2026-09-23 (adopted same day as this research date). The Council voted 5-2 to adopt a resolution starting the moratorium process; while the ordinance is drafted, city planning staff are directed to develop guidelines on water use, power reliability, zoning, noise, and lighting for large-scale data centers, and a work session for the Council to be briefed on impacts is to be scheduled within 90 days. No moratorium ordinance has yet been adopted; per Mayor Mark McBrayer, the near-term practical effect is limited since 'no one's coming to Lubbock in the next year anyway with a data center' given current ERCOT conditions. affected_projects: None named as currently pending before the city.
outcome: Resolution adopted to begin the legal process toward a possible 90-day (optionally extendable to 180-day) data center moratorium, following a citizen petition campaign; the moratorium ordinance itself has not yet been adopted.

date_enacted: County Commission unanimously adopted Ordinance 654 on 2026-06-10.
duration: 180-day temporary land-use regulation on data centers, data center power plants, and associated digital infrastructure in areas where the county retains land-use authority. Stops new land-use and business-license applications, building permits, administrative appeals, conditional use permits, subdivisions, zone changes, site plans, development agreements, and similar approvals. Applications formally determined complete before the effective date may proceed; incomplete covered applications are suspended.
legal_basis: Ordinance 654, Box Elder County Commission
trigger: Adopted while the county develops updated data center regulations, in areas outside the Military Installation Development Authority's Stratos project area.
current_status: Active as of 2026-07-31; 180-day pause from 2026-06-10. County officials expressly stated it does not affect the Stratos project, because the Military Installation Development Authority (MIDA), not the county, controls land use within that project area.
affected_projects: Explicitly does not apply to the Stratos project (MIDA-controlled project area)

legal_basis: Ordinance 2026-32, Cache County Council
trigger: Proactive measure; minutes state the county had received no data center inquiries and the action was not a response to a pending project.
current_status: Active as of 2026-07-31; 180-day pause from 2026-06-23, adopted proactively with no pending data center project.

date_enacted: 2026-09-08, Clearfield City Council regular meeting, 4-0 vote (Councilmember Danielle King absent).
duration: 180 days from adoption (to approximately 2027-03-07).
legal_basis: Temporary land use regulation/moratorium on data center development approved by Clearfield City Council 4-0 on September 8, 2026, following an August 25, 2026 work-session discussion (recorded in the city's own signed minutes) in which the city attorney confirmed the Council could adopt a 180-day temporary land use regulation while a pending zoning-determination request for a data center at Freeport Center Building J8 was evaluated.
trigger: regulatory_gap; a pending zoning-determination request for a proposed data center in the Freeport Center's M-1 Manufacturing Zone (Building J8) exposed that Clearfield's code has no definition or zoning classification for 'data center,' prompting the Council to pause while it studies electrical demand, water consumption, noise, and other impacts and considers pending state legislation.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. The Clearfield City Council voted 4-0 on September 8, 2026 to adopt a 180-day moratorium prohibiting data center development in the city (through approximately March 7, 2027) while officials study whether special zoning guidelines are warranted. No data center proposal was found to be barred outright by the action; a pending zoning-determination request at the Freeport Center (Building J8) prompted the pause. No extension or replacement was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
affected_projects: A pending zoning-determination request (not yet a formal application) for a proposed data center in Building J8 at the Freeport Center, M-1 Manufacturing Zone; city staff's preliminary review found the use did not clearly fit existing warehouse or manufacturing classifications.
outcome: Clearfield City Council adopted a 180-day moratorium on data center development after a zoning-determination request exposed a gap in the city's zoning code.

date_enacted: County Commission voted 7-0 on 2026-07-07 to adopt a temporary land use regulation, effective immediately.
duration: 180-day pause on acceptance and processing of applications for data centers, data center power plants, and associated digital infrastructure. Planning and Zoning Director Andrew Jackson said no data center application was pending and the county code lacked a data center definition and standards addressing water, power, noise, lighting, and visual impacts.
legal_basis: Item 15, 'Ordinance - Temporary land use regulation - Data Centers,' approved 7-0 (Commissioner Bill Winfield's motion seconded, all present commissioners voting yes) at the Grand County Commission's July 7, 2026 regular meeting, per the county's own signed meeting minutes; pauses acceptance and processing of applications, permits, and licenses for data centers, data center power plants, and associated digital infrastructure for up to 180 days. County staff refer to the instrument as a 'temporary land use regulation' rather than 'moratorium' on the advice of the county's land-use attorney, though it functions as a moratorium. No separately numbered ordinance document (e.g., 'Ordinance No. ___') was found; the minutes themselves are the primary record of adoption.
trigger: County code lacked a data center definition and standards addressing water, power, noise, lighting, and visual impacts; no data center application was pending.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Confirmed via Grand County's own signed July 7, 2026 Commission meeting minutes: the Commission voted 7-0 to adopt the ordinance/temporary land use regulation pausing acceptance and processing of data center, data center power plant, and associated digital infrastructure applications for up to 180 days (through approximately January 3, 2027), effective immediately. Staff described it as 'not a ban' and confirmed no data center applications were pending at adoption. No extension, replacement, or rescission was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23. A distinct, unrelated moratorium reported by SkyHiNews.com running through June 2027 refers to Grand County, Colorado, not this Grand County, Utah row.

date_enacted: County Commission approved Ordinance 2026-13 by a 2-0 vote (Commissioner Paul Cozzens absent) on 2026-05-26.

trigger: Adopted while the county develops updated data center and solar power plant regulations.
current_status: Active as of 2026-07-31; 180-day pause from 2026-05-26. This is distinct from the Antelope Data Center conditional-use permit the Planning Commission approved on 2026-06-04, which county staff say was deemed complete before the moratorium took effect and so was not blocked by it.
affected_projects: Pronghorn Development LLC's Antelope Data Center application (deemed complete, exempt); BrightNight's Red Butte Energy and Data Center Campus application (incomplete, placed on hold)

date_enacted: Municipal Council voted 5-0 to adopt Ordinance 26-12 on 2026-06-30, following a public hearing; published and effective 2026-07-01.

current_status: Active as of 2026-07-31; 180-day moratorium effective 2026-07-01.

No extension or replacement was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
affected_projects: None named; no data center application was reported pending in the county at adoption.
outcome: Sanpete County Commission adopted a six-month moratorium on new data center development, directing Planning and Zoning staff to draft permanent land-use regulations.

legal_basis: Resolution 2026-04, Wayne County Commission

date_enacted: 2026-08-31 (Select Board and Village Board of Trustees joint unanimous vote, dated interim zoning bylaw)
duration: Two years from adoption, as an interim zoning bylaw
legal_basis: Interim zoning bylaw adopted unanimously by the Morristown Select Board and Village of Morrisville Board of Trustees, dated 2026-08-31, following a selectboard proposal and two public hearings in August 2026
trigger: Town bylaws are silent on data centers and 'high-impact uses'; board wants time for the planning commission to study electric-grid, water, noise, and hazardous-waste impacts before any application is filed, prompted in part by community reaction to a separate large industrial-park/quarry proposal
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. The interim zoning bylaw (dated 2026-08-31) blocks consideration of applications for data centers and other defined 'high-impact uses' -- facilities that consume 10+ megawatts of power from any source, use 57,600+ gallons of water per day, discharge hazardous waste, add more than 10 acres of impervious surface, or emit more than 70 decibels of persistent noise -- for two years, with an exemption for small data centers necessary for the administrative/operational support of an existing business, hospital, school, municipal service, or residence. Intended to give the planning commission time to draft permanent zoning addressing such uses; runs through approximately 2028-08-31.
affected_projects: None named; officials and residents confirmed no data center has been proposed in Morristown and few parcels are large enough to host one, but the board called the moratorium precautionary.
outcome: Adopted unanimously by the Select Board and Village Board of Trustees on 2026-08-31 after a public hearing with dozens of residents, most supportive; Morristown is the third Vermont community (after Royalton's permanent five-year ban and South Burlington's zoning amendment) to restrict data centers.

date_enacted: 2026-07-21 (City Council adopted Resolution 26-R-042 by a 9-0 vote)
duration: 8 months from adoption, or until City Council takes final action on comprehensive plan amendment PLN-COMP-2026-002, whichever occurs first
legal_basis: Resolution 26-R-042, adopted by Chesapeake City Council 9-0 on July 21, 2026
trigger: Council sought to pause discretionary review of data center land-use applications while comprehensive plan amendment PLN-COMP-2026-002 is pending
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. The Resolution 26-R-042 deferral remains in force, running 8 months from its July 21, 2026 adoption (to approximately 2027-03-21) or until Council takes final action on comprehensive plan amendment PLN-COMP-2026-002, whichever occurs first. On August 18, 2026 the City Council separately and unanimously adopted a zoning ordinance amendment that removes data centers from by-right development, requires a conditional use permit for all future data center proposals in the M-1/M-2 industrial districts, and prohibits data centers from drawing groundwater; this closed a loophole that could have let a data center proceed administratively despite the moratorium, but it is a permanent zoning change layered on top of, not a replacement for, the still-active Resolution 26-R-042 deferral. The zoning change was prompted partly by Praetorian Fund's August 2026 purchase of the Frank Williams Farm Tract (Coastal Virginia Commerce Park); because that site does not connect to public utilities, city officials confirmed the moratorium independently applies to it. No repeal, extension, or expiration of the moratorium itself was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
affected_projects: No single named project; applies citywide to discretionary data center land-use applications pending before the Planning Commission or City Council.
outcome: Enacted deferral of discretionary data center land-use applications pending completion of a related comprehensive plan amendment.

legal_basis: Board motion approving a moratorium on new data center applications; related resolution of intention and ZTA 25:10
trigger: Data centers were by-right uses in I-1 and I-2 districts, and the Board directed staff to prepare amendments requiring special use permits.
current_status: Replaced / expired
affected_projects: No named project or MW total identified in the captured packets; contemporaneous rezoning comments raised concern about possible data center use.
outcome: ZTA 25:10 moved data centers from by-right use to special use permit treatment in I-1 and I-2 and modified the data center definition.

date_enacted: 2026-07-06, Front Royal Town Council work session, 6-0 vote (Vice Mayor Amber F. Veitenthal and Councilmembers DeDomenico-Payne, Ingram, Rappaport, Sealock, and Wood; Mayor Cockrell present but votes only to break ties), per the town's own approved council minutes.
duration: 90 days from adoption (to approximately 2026-10-04).
legal_basis: Resolution Establishing a Temporary Ninety (90) Day Moratorium on the Acceptance of Data Center Land Use Applications, adopted 6-0 by Front Royal Town Council at its July 6, 2026 work session. Town Attorney George Sonnett advised the moratorium was structured as an administrative action (rather than a legislative zoning-ordinance amendment) because, in his opinion, Virginia law does not authorize a legislative moratorium through the zoning ordinance.
trigger: The town sought to preserve the status quo while it drafts a permanent zoning text amendment to define data centers separately from 'technology' uses and prohibit data centers in all town zoning districts; no data center application had been received as of adoption.

The Town Council's July 6, 2026 resolution imposing a 90-day moratorium on accepting data center land-use applications (rezonings, special uses, site development plans) remains in force, with its term running through approximately October 4, 2026. The companion permanent zoning-ordinance prohibition has not yet been adopted: a September 8, 2026 work session reviewed revised ordinance language from outside legal counsel, and the Council decided against setting a public hearing date that month over concerns about the wording, so the permanent measure remains pending as of this research date.
affected_projects: None named; Town Manager Joseph Petty confirmed no data center applications had been received as of the July 6, 2026 vote.
outcome: Front Royal Town Council adopted a 90-day administrative moratorium on data center land-use applications while it drafts a permanent zoning prohibition.

date_enacted: 2026-09-16, Loudoun County Board of Supervisors, 7-1-1 vote (Supervisor opposed on the base pause; a separate 7-1-1 vote with Supervisor Briskman opposed approved a grid-reliability substation exception), per the Board's own press release.
duration: Open-ended; in effect while the Board continues Phase 2 of its Data Center Standards and Locations initiative (zoning ordinance and comprehensive plan amendments), which is anticipated to be completed in 2027. County staff are to return with a formal resolution memorializing the pause at the Board's October 20, 2026 Business Meeting.
legal_basis: Board of Supervisors action taken September 16, 2026 enacting a temporary pause on Board consideration of certain legislative (Special Exception) applications for data centers and substations, pending a formal resolution to be brought to the Board's October 20, 2026 Business Meeting; per the County Attorney, Virginia law does not permit a blanket moratorium on administrative applications, so the pause applies only to legislative applications and does not affect roughly 17 land-use cases (11+ million square feet) 'grandfathered' under the county's March 2025 Data Center Grandfathering Resolution, which continue through the by-right administrative process.
trigger: Regulatory gap and community pressure over rapid data center growth in the county ("Data Center Alley"); effort led by Algonkian District Supervisor Juli Briskman, tied to the county's ongoing Phase 2 Data Center Standards and Locations initiative (begun September 2025) addressing data center/substation siting, noise, building heights, on-site power generation, and battery storage standards.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. The Board of Supervisors voted 7-1-1 on September 16, 2026 to enact, effective immediately, a temporary pause on Board consideration of certain legislative data center and substation applications while Phase 2 of its Data Center Standards and Locations initiative continues; a companion 7-1-1 vote (Briskman opposed) approved an exception allowing consideration of applications involving a 'grid reliability' substation during the pause. The pause does not apply to administratively processed, 'grandfathered' data center cases. A formal resolution memorializing the pause is scheduled to come before the Board at its October 20, 2026 Business Meeting; separately, the Board is set to receive legal analysis on October 6, 2026 on whether the 2025 grandfathering exceptions can be ended for cases that have not yet achieved vested rights.
affected_projects: At least 17 land-use cases representing more than 11 million square feet of data center development are 'grandfathered' under the county's March 2025 resolution and continue through by-right administrative review, unaffected by this pause.
outcome: Loudoun County Board of Supervisors enacted an immediate, open-ended pause on Board consideration of most new legislative data center and substation applications while it completes Phase 2 of its data center zoning and siting standards.

date_enacted: 2026-08-18, Virginia Beach City Council, unanimous vote.
duration: 12 months from adoption, or until City Council takes final action on an ordinance regulating data centers, whichever occurs first (to approximately 2027-08-18).
legal_basis: Resolution adopted by Virginia Beach City Council on August 18, 2026, pausing the issuance of permits related to any new data center for 12 months or until Council takes final action on an ordinance regulating data centers, whichever occurs first; follows planning staff's finding that data centers are currently classified, by default, as wholesaling/warehousing/storage/distribution uses permitted by right in industrial districts.
trigger: City zoning ordinance does not specifically define or regulate data centers; concerns raised over resource consumption (water, electricity), noise, and land-use compatibility, following an informal June 2026 Council statement opposing large-scale/hyperscale data centers.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. Virginia Beach City Council unanimously adopted a 12-month moratorium on new data center permits on August 18, 2026, the same night Chesapeake City Council closed its by-right loophole. The moratorium does not affect existing facilities such as Globalinx's subsea-cable colocation operations, and is intended to apply to future larger-scale and hyperscale data center proposals while the city studies zoning definitions, setbacks, and noise standards. No repeal, extension, or replacement ordinance was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
affected_projects: No large-scale storage/computing data center currently operates in Virginia Beach; existing subsea-cable landing and carrier-neutral colocation facilities (e.g., Globalinx) are not affected.
outcome: Virginia Beach City Council unanimously adopted a 12-month moratorium on new data center permits while it develops zoning definitions and regulations for the industry.

date_enacted: 2026-03-03 (interim zoning controls prohibiting BESS citywide, Ordinance No. 26-1246, superseding an earlier BESS permit-application moratorium first adopted 2024-02-15 under Ordinance No. 24-1205 and renewed by Ordinance No. 25-1219 in February 2025); extended a further six months, with a small-system exception, by Ordinance No. 26-1258 (public hearing scheduled 2026-10-06)

legal_basis: Black Diamond Ordinance No. 26-1246 (adopted 2026-03-03), adopting interim zoning controls prohibiting battery energy storage systems in all zones (amending BDMC 18.100.710); succeeded an earlier permit-application moratorium (Ordinance No. 24-1205, 2024-02-15, renewed by Ordinance No. 25-1219 in Feb. 2025).
