affected_projects: Not identified; originated from a developer's pre-application inquiry rather than a filed permit
outcome: Black Diamond converted its earlier BESS permit-application moratorium into interim zoning controls outright prohibiting BESS citywide (Ordinance No. 26-1246, 2026-03-03), then extended that prohibition a further six months with a small-system exception (Ordinance No. 26-1258).

date_enacted: 2018-10-17 (Spokesman-Review reported the "City Council voted Wednesday" of 2018-10-17 to block new cryptocurrency operations for 12 months; vote 6-1 with Mayor Reim absent)
duration: 12 months (per Spokesman-Review: "yearlong ban on new cryptocurrency mining")
legal_basis: Interim moratorium adopted by City Council vote on 2018-10-17 (per Spokesman-Review); later codified and superseded within Ephrata Municipal Code (EMC) Chapter 19.30 'High Intensity Computer Operations,' whose legislative-history citation reads '(Ord 18-13, 2018; Ord 18-28, 2018).' Note: EMC 19.02's definition of 'high intensity computer operations' expressly excludes the exchange of cryptocurrency/virtual currency and peer-to-peer distributed-ledger maintenance, so the permanent code is framed as a broader high-density-computing-load prohibition rather than a cryptocurrency-specific one.
trigger: Grant County PUD power-capacity uncertainty (Grant PUD received 125 service requests totaling >2,000 MW with ~75% from cryptocurrency firms), noise complaints from residents on Nob Hill Drive ("the noise was like an ocean"), and local concern over whether cryptocurrency mining fit the city utility and land-use framework
current_status: Replaced. The 2018 temporary cryptocurrency-mining moratorium was superseded the same year by a permanent citywide prohibition on 'High Intensity Computer Operations' (EMC 19.30.010: 'All high intensity computer operations shall be prohibited within the City of Ephrata, including those conducted as a home occupation'), citing Ordinance 18-13 (2018) and Ordinance 18-28 (2018), confirmed via the City's own published Municipal Code as of 2026-09-23.
affected_projects: Four existing cryptocurrency operations were reported (two at the Port of Ephrata, one in a city-zoned industrial area, and one in a residential area being relocated); the moratorium applied to new operations only

current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23. That referendum was held as scheduled and was defeated: of 1,184 votes cast, 87.25% (1,033) voted "No" on whether the Village should authorize, support, or facilitate public resources or infrastructure for a large-scale data center development (a non-binding result that does not itself alter the moratorium). No repeal, rescission, or replacement of the July 7 moratorium ordinance was found as of 2026-09-23. duration: 12 months
legal_basis: Ordinance 26-01 (Town of Westport, Dane County), "Establishing a Temporary Moratorium on the Consideration and/or Issuance of Permits for [Data Centers and Telecommunication Centers]"
trigger: Modeled on a similar moratorium passed by the City of Madison; adopted amid growing data center prospecting activity in Dane County.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; adopted April 6, 2026 on a motion by Werner, seconded by Crowell, with Supervisor Manering dissenting (she wanted the ordinance to apply to all data centers regardless of size). Applies to data centers exceeding 10,000 square feet; covers a one-year moratorium on considering or issuing permits for data centers and telecommunication centers.
outcome: Adopted 12-month moratorium (Ordinance 26-01) on permits for data centers exceeding 10,000 square feet.

date_enacted: August 18, 2026 (County Board voice vote, one dissenting supervisor)
duration: 12 months
legal_basis: Winnebago County data center moratorium ordinance (ordinance number not located in reviewed sources), enacted under Wis. Stat. § 59.69(4)
trigger: No county mechanism to regulate data centers; concerns over energy/water use, noise pollution, and utility rate impacts amid a wave of similar Wisconsin county and city moratoria.
current_status: Active as of 2026-09-23; passed in a voice vote at the Aug. 18, 2026 meeting, with District 24 Supervisor Andy Buck as the lone apparent dissenter (his prior motion to shorten the term to 6 months failed). Applies only in the four townships where the county has general zoning authority: Algoma, Omro, Neenah, and Nekimi; cities such as Oshkosh, Neenah, and Menasha must adopt their own regulations.
outcome: Adopted 12-month moratorium on new data center development in the four county-zoned townships.
